game/chapters/night0/dialogue/agnes.talk.name: Agnes
notes: Agnes, Hob's wife, by the fire in the Cross Keys, night 0. Motherly, and sharp.
The bed answer gives him the room at the top (n0_room). An ale ends the talk with her own line; the next talk starts at again, so he can have another.
The ale is always the last answer. Once the bed and the abbey are asked she has one thing more (Jankin), and "(Nod.)" ends the talk with her line.

lines.text: (A woman by the fire with her sleeves rolled, stirring a pot. She looks you up and down.)
Look at you, wet to the skin. Come by the fire before you catch your death.
Your room's made up, brother. Top of the stair, as far as it goes.
Well? Warmer?

answers.text: Have you a bed for the night, goodwife?
What do you know of the abbey?
An ale, if you would.
Is Jankin always like this?
(Nod.)
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: There's the room at the top. It's small and it's cold, and its one window looks toward the abbey.
Nobody else will have it. It's yours for a ha'penny, and I'll not haggle with a monk.
Be in before the curfew bell at nine. After it the Keys is shut, and the street's no place to be.
I don't talk about that place under my own roof.
(She glances at the shutters all the same, and lowers her voice.)
We've had lodgers go over there to see the relic. Paid me for two nights, and slept one.
I don't ask. I strip the bed and let it again.
(She looks down the bench at him, and her face softens.)
Jankin? Every night. Hob puts him out at closing, and I put a crust in his pocket first.
One of these nights it'll be too cold for him out there. You see if it isn't.
Then sit and dry. If you're still down here at midnight, I'll send you up myself.
(She fills a cup from the jug and puts it into your hands.)
Drink it slow. It's stronger than what your country brothers brew.
(She fills it to the brim, shaking her head.)
You'll be no use to your abbot in the morning.
Before nine, mind!

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/carter.tal.name: the carter
notes: The carter sets the porter down in the lane by the abbey gate at dusk, night 0 (RideBeat), then drives off down the lane with the traveller (the scene does that once the talk ends).
Gruff and in a hurry: one answer, one reply, and he's gone. Each reply is his parting line.

lines.text: (The carter twists round on his seat as you climb down. The horse stamps in the wet.)
There's your abbey, brother. I've a horse to stable before dark.

answers.text: Will you wait while I knock, friend?
Is the gate always shut like this?
God keep you, friend.

lines.text: Wait? In this lane, with the light going?
(He spits over the wheel.)
No, brother. Knock all you like. I'll not be here to see it.
Couldn't say. I don't stop here.
(He jerks his head across the lane, at a lit doorway under a painted sign.)
There's the Keys, if they won't have you.
And you. You'll want Him more than I will.
I said down you get. I'm away.
Mind your bundle, brother.

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/gib.talk.name: Gib the watchman
notes: Gib, the old night watchman, night 0: lighting the lanterns along the lane (the mayor's order) before the bell, and walking the lane calling the hour after it (n0_curfew). Old, slow, a watchman: he tells the porter to be indoors before the bell.
His call is a clock the porter will hear from inside the walls: if it stops, something is wrong.
One talk: the questions left come up again until all are asked; then he sends him indoors (done, before or after the bell).

lines.text: (An old man on a short ladder under the eaves, coaxing a lantern alight with a taper.)
Mind my ladder, brother. Gib, the watch. A lantern on every house all winter, by the mayor's order.
And you be indoors before the bell. Nine o'clock, and not a breath after.
(An old man with a lantern on a pole, walking slow down the middle of the empty lane.)
Past the bell, brother, and you in the street. I'm Gib, the watch. Get you indoors.
Still out, brother? Not long to the bell now.
You again, and the bell long gone.

answers.text: What do you do after the bell, friend?
How long has the lane had lanterns?
What do you make of the abbey wall?

lines.text: After the bell I walk the lane and call the hour. Ten of the clock, and on till first light.
If you hear me call, all's well. If you don't, it isn't.
Since the year of Agincourt. Every winter, from Hallowtide to Candlemas.
The houses find the candles, and I light them. Saves a few throats, the mayor says.
(He's slow to answer.)
I walk past that wall every hour of the night, and I don't look at it.
Thirty years. You hear things over a wall like that. You see lights where there shouldn't be lights.
I call the hour, and I keep walking. You'd do well to learn the same.
Well. These lanterns won't light themselves. Indoors before the bell, brother.
That's enough talk for a cold night. Indoors with you, brother.
Get you indoors, brother!

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/hob.talk.name: Hob
notes: Hob, who keeps the Cross Keys, behind his board, night 0. Blunt and kind. He hears everything said over the ale, and doesn't say any of it is true.
His questions: what the lane says about the abbey; when the Keys shuts; who's drinking tonight (once one of the first two is asked). He never runs out: the ale is always there.

The ale is always the last answer, and the third while he has two questions left (always, until he's asked: the tests take answer 2 for an ale). Once the abbey and the shutting are asked, "(Nod.)" ends the talk with his line. An ale ends the talk with his own line; the next talk starts at again, so he can have another.
Plants the night-2 rule (n0_hob_jankin): he puts Jankin out at closing every night, rain or no.

lines.text: (A big man behind the board, a cloth over his shoulder. He looks at your habit a long while before your face.)
A brother from over the way, in the Keys. That's new.
Sit where you like. Not on Jankin.
Brother. What'll it be?

answers.text: What does the lane say about the abbey?
When do you shut, friend?
An ale, if you would.
When do you shut, friend?
Who's drinking here tonight?
An ale, if you would.
What does the lane say about the abbey?
Who's drinking here tonight?
An ale, if you would.
Who's drinking here tonight?
(Nod.)
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: I pour, folk talk. I don't say any of it's true.
Pilgrims go in at that gate and don't come out. Folk say they leave by some back way. I don't know of one.
Lights moving in there at night, at hours no bell's rung for. And a thing up on the wall with horns, Jankin says.
Jankin says a deal. But I keep my shutters barred on that side.
At the bell. After it the door's barred, and it stays barred.
Them with a bed go up the stair. Them without go out. Jankin too, every night, rain or no.
If it's a bed you're after, that's Agnes's business. Don't haggle. She'll win.
(He nods round the room, one face at a time.)
Walter, in the red, selling bones. Roger, the ward's bailiff, with the staff. Ralph the chandler, who makes your candles.
And Jankin, who's always here. Mind what you say near Roger. He counts everything.
Go and sit, then. You're making the place look holy.
(He draws a cup from the cask and sets it down in front of you, hard.)
A ha'penny. Or a prayer for my mother, God rest her. From you I'll take the prayer.
(Down the bench, Jankin's eyes are on your cup.)
Mind Jankin doesn't drink it. I put him out at closing every night, rain or no.
(He pours it, slower than before.)
That's three, brother. Go steady. Agnes won't carry you up the stair.
(He fills your cup again.)
There. Drink it sitting down.
Bell's at nine, brother.

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/jankin.tal.name: Jankin
notes: Jankin on the bench at the Cross Keys, night 0. A harmless drunk, rambling, full of stories, half of them nonsense. Once, for a moment, he isn't drunk at all (who).
He saw a thing with horns on the abbey wall (the horned costume; nothing here says so). He says Hob throws him out at closing every night (the night-2 rule).
One talk: the questions left come up again until all are asked; then he runs out of stories (done).

lines.text: (A man slumped on the bench by the wall lifts his cup to you. Most of it goes down his sleeve.)
A monk! In the Keys! Hob, the world's ending. I always said it would.
Did I tell you about the thing on the wall? I did. It's still true.
Brother! You came back. Nobody comes back to Jankin.

answers.text: What do you know of the abbey, friend?
Who are you, friend?
Where will you sleep tonight?

lines.text: The abbey. I'll tell you about the abbey. I saw a thing on its wall.
Up on the top, by the corner, against the moon. Horns on it like a hart's. Still as a post.
I said good evening to it. It never said good evening back. Rude, I call that.
Hob says it was the drink. Hob says everything's the drink.
Jankin. I was a cooper once, brother. Best barrels in Aldgate.
Then my wife died, and I found I liked what goes in a barrel better than the barrel.
(He looks into his cup, and for a moment he doesn't look drunk at all.)
Never mind. Ask me another.
Tonight? Wherever I fall. Hob throws me out at closing, every night, rain or no.
Good man, Hob. Big hands. I go out of that door like a sack of meal.
There's a step by the chandler's. Dry, mostly. Nobody's murdered me on it yet.
(He peers into his cup.)
That's all my stories, brother. Well. Most of them. Come back when I've thought of the rest.
Pray for me, brother! Somebody ought to.

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/kit.talk.name: Kit
notes: Kit, Ralph the chandler's daughter, selling her last candles in the lane at dusk, night 0. Young, quick, curious about the new porter: she asks more than she answers.
One talk: the questions left come up again until all are asked; then she's off to sell her last two (done).

lines.text: (A girl with a tray of candles on a strap round her neck, her hood up against the rain.)
Candles! Last of the day, two for a farthing. You're a brother. Are you the new porter?
You came back! Two left, brother. Both for a farthing, and I'll throw in the tray.

answers.text: I'm the new porter. Alric.
Who makes your candles?
Have you been inside the abbey?

lines.text: I knew it! Everybody knew you were coming. Gib told Margery, and Margery told the lane.
You're younger than Brother Anselm. Well. Everybody's younger than Brother Anselm.
Father makes them and I sell them. Ralph the chandler. He's in the Keys, most like. I'm Kit.
I'm at your gate most dusks with the tray. The brothers buy whatever I've got left.
Brother Ranulf would buy the tray and the strap, if I let him.
Past the gate? Never. Father says I'm not to, not ever.
Is it true there's a saint's finger in a glass box? And lights going about at night? You'll tell me, when you've seen.
Two candles left, and the light going. I'll see you at your gate, porter!
See you at the gate!

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/mab.talk.name: Mab
notes: Mab, a leper, begging by the barred abbey gate at dusk, night 0. Plain and unflinching: she sees everyone who goes in and out, and nobody asks her. Her first lines send him to the Cross Keys (n0_sent_to_inn).
Alms once (n0_mab_alms): she gives him a heel of bread from a Fenchurch Street baker. She doesn't eat what comes out of the abbey's gate.
One talk: the questions left come up again until all are asked; then she sends him on (done).

lines.text: (A wooden clapper, knocking. A woman sits against the wall by the gate, her face wrapped to the eyes in grey cloth.)
No use knocking, brother. Nobody will come. Nobody keeps that gate at night, not since old Brother Anselm went blind.
Go across to the Cross Keys, there, with the lantern. Agnes will find you a bed.
You again, brother. The Keys hasn't moved.

answers.text: I'm to be their new porter.
Are you here every night?
(Give her a coin.)

lines.text: (She looks at you a long while over the cloth.)
Their porter. You're very young.
I'm Mab. You'll be in there, and I'll be out here. We'll see a deal of each other.
Every night God sends. Rain or frost, it's all one to me.
I see everyone who goes in at that gate, and everyone who comes out. Nobody asks me. Who asks a leper anything?
But I'll tell you for nothing, brother. More go in than come out.
(You drop a penny in the bowl at her feet.)
God keep you, brother. Here. You'll want something for your supper.
(She sets a heel of bread on the step between you, wrapped in a cloth, and draws back.)
It's from a baker on Fenchurch Street. I don't eat what comes out of that gate.
Go on across to the fire, brother. I'll be here. I'm always here.
Mind the lane after the bell, brother.

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/margery.ta.name: Margery
notes: Margery, a neighbour from by Saint Andrew's, hurrying home with her basket before dark, night 0. Hurried, careful, frightened: she won't stop long, and she won't pass the abbey wall after dark.
One talk: she answers what's left until it's all asked, then hurries off (done). Blessing her is a goodbye, and she takes it as one.

lines.text: (A woman with a covered basket on her arm, walking fast, her eyes on the cobbles.)
Can't stop, brother, I'm sorry. Not with the light going.
You again, brother. Quickly, then.

answers.text: Where are you hurrying to?
What are you afraid of?
Go with God, then.

lines.text: Home, by Saint Andrew's. I'm Margery. I go the long way round.
Two streets more, but it doesn't pass that wall.
Afraid? I'm careful, that's all.
(Her eyes go to the abbey wall, and away.)
Even the dogs cross the lane rather than go by it. I don't walk past it after dark. No offence to your habit.
And you, brother. God keep you. You'll need keeping, over there.
(She hitches the basket higher on her arm.)
I must go, brother. God keep you.
God keep you!

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/ralph.talk.name: Ralph the chandler
notes: Ralph the chandler at the Cross Keys, night 0. He makes the abbey's candles; his daughter Kit sells them. A careful tradesman who notices numbers.
The sacrist has bought twice the wax since about Michaelmas, and pays in silver the abbey never used to have (n0_ralph_candles: night 2's Ranulf answers to it).
One talk: the questions left come up again until all are asked; then he goes back to his ale (done).

lines.text: (A thin man with wax under his nails and old burns on his fingers, nursing a small ale.)
From the abbey, are you? Then you're my best customer, brother, whether you know it or not.
Brother. Tell your sacrist I've wax enough for whatever he wants.

answers.text: Your best customer, friend? How so?
How does the sacrist pay you?
How goes your trade?

lines.text: Ralph, chandler. Every candle in that church came out of my shop.
At Easter your sacrist, Brother Ranulf, bought a dozen pound of wax a month. Since Michaelmas, two dozen, and more.
I asked him once what they burn it all for. He didn't say.
In silver. On the nail, and he doesn't haggle.
That abbey hadn't two pennies to rub together. Everybody knew it. Now it's silver.
I don't ask where a man of God gets his silver. I'm a chandler. I sell candles.
Wax for the altar, tallow for the rest. It's a living, if you don't mind the stink.
My girl Kit sells them in the lane. She's at your gate most dusks with her tray. Be kind to her.
That's all I know, brother, and more than a chandler ought to say. Good night to you.
Good night, brother. Pray for the price of wax.

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/roger.talk.name: Roger the bailiff
notes: Roger, bailiff of the ward, drinking at the Cross Keys, night 0. Officious, counting, cold: he has counted the porter before he sits down.
He wants word of any merchant, anyone with money, who goes in at the abbey gate (n0_roger_agreed if the porter says he'll send it). The ward would like the abbey's land.
Claims: n0_roger_count (hiding): why he wants the names. True as far as it goes; he leaves out the land. Pressed, he hints at it.
One talk: after he has asked his favour, the questions left come up again until all are asked; then he dismisses him (done). Not agreeing is allowed: the offer stays open and he walks away.

lines.text: (A broad man in a good brown coat, a staff of office leaning on the table. He was watching you before you came in.)
You came in on the carter's wagon, in a habit, with one bundle. Who are you?

answers.text: Brother Alric, the abbey's new porter.
Who's asking, friend?
(Say nothing.)

lines.text: The new porter. So they found one at last. I'm Roger, bailiff of this ward.
Roger, bailiff of this ward. When I ask, people answer. You'll be their new porter.
A habit, a bundle, and a face that's never seen London. You're their new porter.
I'm Roger, bailiff of this ward. It's my business to know who comes into it.
Merchants come to that gate. Pilgrims with fat purses.
When one goes in, I'd like to hear of it. His name, and where he's from. That's all.
A merchant, a name. You know where I drink.
Porter. Thought on what I asked?

answers.text: Why do you want to know?
I'll send you word.
What does the ward want with the abbey?

lines.text: Because men with money go in there, and the ward never hears of them again.
Somebody ought to keep count. Your abbey doesn't.

answers.text: Then we want the same thing, you and I.
A bailiff, keeping count of pilgrims for nothing?

lines.text: Then we understand each other. Names, porter. That's all I ask.
(He looks at you a while.)
You're not as green as your habit.
A house that loses its guests can lose other things. The ward keeps count of those as well.
Good. A porter who keeps count is worth something to the ward. The ward pays its friends.
The ward wants nothing. The ward is patient.
That's good land behind your wall. Too good for an abbey that can't keep count of its own guests.
If your abbey ever falls on hard times, there are men on the ward who'd put it to better use. Remember who told you.
That's all I wanted, porter. One merchant, one name. I'll know where to find you.
Think on it, porter. The ward remembers its friends.

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/traveller..name: Traveller
notes: The traveller (Will Fuller) beside the porter on the carter's wagon, night 0. The carter has pulled in; as the cart with the dead comes close the traveller breaks off whatever he was saying (traveller_road.talk is that talk) and turns to it. It opens on him, not on a greeting: they have been talking all the way from the fields.
Four pilgrims under sacking, found in the ditch: seven this month on this road. They went in at the abbey's gate to see the saint; nobody saw them come out; they turn up after, outside the walls.
The ride reveals nothing of what or who is behind it: no demon, no men, no robbery. Only the dead, the count, the abbey, and a man too frightened to say what people say.
If the porter told him he's the abbey's porter (n0_road_porter), he says your abbey; if not, the carter has told him.

One talk: the questions left come up again until all are asked; then he watches the cart go and closes it (done). What he doesn't get to say here (Aldgate may cut it short), the porter can ask him after (traveller_road.talk, after).

lines.text: Whoa. Look at that.
(The cart creaks by close enough to touch. Shapes lie under sacking on its bed, three side by side and one across them.)
God's wounds. That's not one man. That's four.

answers.text: God rest them. Who were they?
What happened to them?
(Cross yourself.)

lines.text: Pilgrims, by the badges on their hats. Nobody knows them. Nobody ever does.
Men from the shires who saved a year to see a saint, and nobody here to ask after them.
Found in the ditch, the carter says. All four together, in the one ditch.
Not a mark on them. As if they'd lain down there to sleep.
(You say the words for the dead under your breath. The traveller's lips move with yours.)
Say one for yourself while you're at it.
That makes seven this month, on this road alone. Every one of them bound for your abbey, to see the saint.
That makes seven this month, on this road alone. The carter says you're for the abbey in the lane.
That's where they were all bound. To see the saint.

answers.text: Why lay it at the abbey's door?
What do people say?
I'll see for myself what's there.

lines.text: They go in at that gate to see the saint. Nobody sees them come out.
Then a week on, a month on, they turn up in a ditch outside the walls. Like those.
(He crosses himself.)
I don't say how. I don't know how. Nobody does.
(He opens his mouth, and shuts it again.)
People say a good many things, brother. None of them in daylight.
You'll hear it all at the Keys tonight. I'd rather not be the one who told you.
You will, brother. That's what worries me.
(The cart's lantern goes small down the road behind you. The traveller doesn't take his eyes off it.)
God keep you better than He kept those, brother.
I can still see that cart, brother. Ask, if you want to.
Look away, then. I wish I could.

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/traveller_.name: Traveller
notes: The traveller beside the porter on the carter's wagon, night 0: Will Fuller, a wool merchant from Colchester, forty-one, bound for Cheapside, inside the walls. A wife and two girls at home. Wry and warm, and more frightened than he lets on.
He turns to the porter himself a little way down the road (the Fields cue), and the porter can turn to him again on the road in (E): that starts at again.
One turn to him is one talk: after each answer the questions left come up again, until the porter turns away or has asked them all; then he closes it himself (spent, after_spent).

Before the cart he only hints: road talk, men who set out for London and don't come home. When the cart with the dead comes close he breaks this talk off himself (traveller.talk says the rest), with no parting line; at Aldgate he breaks off again to greet the warden.

After the cart (talked_n0_traveller) the porter can ask what he thinks goes on in the abbey, what people say, and who would know more. Nothing on the ride reveals a demon or men behind the deaths. After Aldgate (n0_past_aldgate) he opens on the warden.

lines.text: (The man on the seat beside you, a merchant by his good wet cloak, has watched the road go by in silence. Now he turns to you.)
Evening, brother. Bound for the city, are you?

answers.text: I'm to be porter at an abbey inside Aldgate.
Where are you bound yourself, friend?
(Nod.)

lines.text: Not one for talk. Then I'll talk for both of us. It keeps the cold out.
The porter? At the abbey in the lane, across from the Cross Keys?
(He looks at you a moment longer than he needs to.)
Well. Somebody has to keep the gate. You look young for it, though.

answers.text: I'm nineteen. Old enough.
The old porter went blind.
I go where my abbot sends me.

lines.text: Nineteen. At nineteen I was sure I'd be rich by thirty.
I'm forty-one, and sat in the back of a cart in the rain. Keep your vows, brother. They're cheaper than wool.
(He's quiet a moment.)
Years on a gate, watching who comes in after dark. Maybe the eyes just give up.
Obedience. My father wanted that of me, and got a wool trade instead.
Does your abbot know the house he's sending you to?

answers.text: He says it's a holy house, with a saint.
I don't think he knows it at all.

lines.text: A saint. Yes. Everyone on this road has heard of the saint.
(He says it the way a man names a dog that once bit him.)
Then that's two of you who don't. Three, with me.
Cheapside, with wool. Three days from Colchester, and every one of them wet.
Every toll on the road robs me. The bridges, the gates, the bishop's men. A sack's half spent before it's sold.

answers.text: Have you family at home?
Is it a good living?
(Nod.)

lines.text: (He nods at the sacks behind you.)
Good enough to grumble about. Those are a winter's bread for my house.
Which is why I'll sleep inside the walls tonight, and not in some ditch.
A wife, and two girls who think London's paved with ribbon. I'm to bring them some.
(His face goes quiet.)
My wife made me swear I'd stop nowhere but an inn I know. She's heard the stories.

answers.text: What stories?
(Nod.)

lines.text: Road talk. Men set out for London and don't come home. There are always a few.
(He glances at the carter's back.)
More, this year. Ask him why he whips his horse when the light goes.
They shut the city gates at the curfew bell. Be on the wrong side and you sleep in the ditch.
He doesn't care to sleep in a ditch. Not this month.
Will Fuller. Will, to anyone who's shared a wet cart with me.
And you're Brother Something, and you'll tell me if you like. I'll not press a monk.

answers.text: I'm Alric.
(Smile.)

lines.text: Alric. Well, Brother Alric. I'll pray for you, if you'll pray for my wool.

answers.text: I'm to be porter at an abbey inside Aldgate.
Where are you bound yourself, friend?
Why is the carter in such a hurry?
I never asked your name, friend.
Why is the carter in such a hurry?
What's different about this year?

lines.text: (He shifts on his seat.)
Go on, brother, ask. It shortens the road.
(He pulls his hood closer.)
Save your breath, brother. It's a cold way to Aldgate yet.
Still thinking of that cart, brother? So am I.
He took his time over you, that warden. Most nights they wave a monk through.

answers.text: What do you think goes on in that abbey?
What do people say about it?
Who would know more?

lines.text: I think men go in at that gate to pray, and nobody sees them come out.
That's all I know, and it's more than I want to.

answers.text: Those are my brothers you speak of.
Have you been inside?
(Say nothing.)

lines.text: I'm speaking of a wall I can't see over. You'll be over it tomorrow. Then you tell me.
Once, at Lent, to see the saint. A finger in a glass box, and more candles than I'd seen in my life.
And cold in there, like the bottom of a well. I said my prayer and I didn't stay.
(He opens his mouth, and shuts it again.)
People say a good many things, brother. None of them in daylight.
You'll hear it all at the Keys tonight. I'd rather not be the one who told you.
The Cross Keys, across the lane from your gate. Buy the landlord an ale and he'll talk till the candle's out.
His wife hears more, and says less.
(He tries a smile.)
I've said more than I meant to, brother. It's the cold. It loosens a man.
Suit yourself, brother.

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/walter.tal.name: Walter
notes: Walter the pardoner at the Cross Keys, night 0, selling relics to the drinkers out of a rattling box. A salesman: flattering, never still, and he calls himself Walter. His baseline is amused, with a flick of the brow; his tell is that he stops selling.
He knows the abbey's gate well and won't say why. (He supplies the henbane. Nothing here says so.)
Claims: n0_walter_gate (hiding): what his business at the abbey gate is. Pressed, he stops selling for a moment and says herbs for the brothers, no more. Believed, he never says.
One talk: the questions left come up again until all are asked; then he turns back to the drinkers (done).

lines.text: (A plump man in a wine-red cloak, the only colour in the room. The box on his knees rattles when he moves.)
A brother! Come and sit by Walter. Walter has something for every soul in the Keys, and you've a soul, I'll be bound.
Back to Walter! They always come back.

answers.text: (Look in his box.)
Do you know the abbey, Walter?
What business have you at the abbey gate?

lines.text: (He lifts the lid. Little bones, scraps of cloth and a cloudy phial, each on its own bed of wool.)
A tooth of Saint Apollonia, for the toothache. A thread of Our Lady's veil.
And this, a drop of her milk, from Walsingham. A groat to you, since you're in the trade.

answers.text: I have no money, Walter.
Those aren't holy.
(Shake your head.)

lines.text: No money! Of course. Your vows. Walter forgets.
(He shuts the lid gently, as if on something sleeping.)
Keep Walter in your prayers, then, and a kind eye on him at your gate. We'll call it square.
(He is still smiling.)
Holy enough for Aldgate. Faith does the rest, brother. Faith always does.
Know it? I know every gate in London, and that one best of all.
You'll be the new porter. Don't look so struck, brother. Word gets about, in the trade.
You and Walter will be friends. Walter's at that gate more nights than not.
Oh, this and that. Things the brothers can't grow in their own garden.
(He pats the box. Something inside it rattles.)
Holy business, brother. Nothing a porter need trouble his head over.

answers.text: Then I'll not trouble it.
What things, Walter? I'm the one who'll open the gate to them.

lines.text: Spoken like a porter! Walter knew you had sense.
(For a moment he stops selling. The smile goes, and comes back.)
Herbs, brother. Dried, in little bags, for the brothers who ask for them. A pardoner carries what he's asked to carry.
There. Now you know all Walter knows, and Walter knows nothing.
(He turns back to the drinkers, and his box.)
Now, Walter has souls to see to. Till the gate, brother!
Walter will see you at the gate, brother!

game/chapters/night0/dialogue/warden.tal.name: Warden
notes: The warden at Aldgate, night 0. The wagon has stopped, he has walked up beside the porter and holds his lantern up to his face (RideBeat, the Aldgate cue's inspector). When the talk ends he lowers it and walks back to his place saying they can go (the cue's parting_lines): that is the talk's closing line, so his own last answer can end it.

A gatekeeper talking to a gatekeeper: blunt and tired. He lifts the sacking on every cart that passes his gate, and has counted the dead this month. Nothing he says names a demon or men behind the deaths.
His one question asked (or a nod), the talk ends.

lines.text: (He holds his lantern up to your face, and looks at you a long moment.)
A monk, and a young one. Where are you bound, brother?

answers.text: To the abbey in the lane. I'm to be its porter.
To the abbey in the lane.
(Say nothing.)

lines.text: (The lantern doesn't move.)
The porter. The old one went blind, I heard.
You'll keep your gate and I'll keep mine. Mine shuts at the curfew bell. Does yours?

answers.text: It will now.
I don't know yet.

lines.text: Good. Bar it at the bell, and don't open it to a knock till it's light. Not for anyone.
Then learn that before you learn anything else. Bar it at the bell, and keep it barred till it's light.
(His mouth goes thin.)
Pilgrim?

answers.text: No. I'm sent to keep its gate.
Just a monk, friend.

lines.text: Just a monk. There's no such thing in this city, brother.
Light in your eyes? It's meant to be. A face tells me more than a mouth does.
Yours says you've never slept inside a city wall.

answers.text: You saw the cart with the dead, warden?
(Nod.)

lines.text: I see every cart, brother. I lift the sacking, and I count.
Seven this month. Most of them came in at this gate on their own feet, to see your saint.
I've seen you, brother. Go on through.
Look away all you like. I've seen what I need.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/anselm.tal.name: Brother Anselm
notes: Anselm, the old porter, by the infirmary brazier at dusk (night 1). Blind, guilty and terrified: he hints, never tells.
He wants to know the porter remembers his warning from the tour (d1_anselm_warned). If the tour was skipped, he gives it now.
Hint: by the old porter who locked the guests in, he meant himself, and he didn't, every night.

lines.text: (The old porter sits by the brazier with a blanket round him. His white eyes are on the door before you're through it.)
That's the porter's step. The keys give you away. I wore them thirty years.
(He listens to the room a moment, then leans toward you.)
This morning, when we were alone. What I told you. You remember it?

answers.text: Don't let them in after the bell.
You said the old porter locked the guests in.
Why? What happens after the bell?

lines.text: (He lets out his breath.)
Good lad. Say it over when they knock. Say it like a psalm.
I said the old porter. I meant me.
I locked them in. Most nights. (He turns his face away.) Lock them in, porter. Every night.
(His hand finds your sleeve and holds it.)
Because I did. Don't ask me more. Not here.
(He listens to the room a moment, then his hand finds your sleeve.)
Don't let them in after the bell. Whatever they tell you.
And lock the guesthouse at night. The old porter always did.
(He turns his face toward you.)
Still here? Go on to your supper. They'll notice if you're late.
After the bell, porter. Remember.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/choira.tal.name: Brother Wulfric
notes: Brother Wulfric, the oldest of the choir, on the south walk at dusk (night 1). Background; short and crabbed.

lines.text: (An old brother of the choir on the south walk, rubbing his knees against the cold.)
So you're the porter. Ring Matins on the mark, boy. Old knees need warning.
The bell, boy. On the mark.

answers.text: How long have you sung here, brother?

lines.text: Forty years. I've seen porters come, and I've seen them go. Most of them go.
On the mark, mind.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/choirb.tal.name: Brother Aldo
notes: Brother Aldo, a young brother of the choir, in the nave at dusk (night 1). Background; friendly.

lines.text: (A young brother in the nave, humming a chant under his breath. He stops when he sees you.)
Sorry. Tonight's psalm. I come in a beat behind Wulfric every night, and he never forgives me.
Matins, porter. Ring it loud.

answers.text: How do I count the brothers at Matins?

lines.text: Count the stalls. An empty one's a man still abed, and it's the porter who goes to fetch him.
Loud, mind. Wulfric's half deaf.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/choirc.tal.name: Brother Piers
notes: Brother Piers, of the choir, on the east walk at dusk (night 1), watching the rain fill the garden. Background.

lines.text: (A brother of the choir on the east walk, watching the rain drown the garden beds.)
They say you're from the country. You'll find London's rain is the same, only dirtier.
Still raining. It always is, in November.

answers.text: What's the house like, brother?

lines.text: Quiet. We were thirty once, the old brothers say. Now look at us.
Keep dry, porter.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/cole.talk.name: Cole
notes: Cole, the lay brother, keeping the gate at dusk (night 1). Big and silent: a word or two at most, and a look.

lines.text: (Cole stands in the gate's arch with the rain running off his hood. He looks at you, then at the keys on your belt.)
(Cole looks at you and says nothing.)

answers.text: I'll take the gate after supper.
Did anyone come to the gate today?

lines.text: After supper.
(He nods once, and goes back to watching the lane.)
(He thinks about it.)
Candle girl.
(Cole watches you go.)

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/dunstan.ta.name: Dunstan
notes: Dunstan, the lay brother, splitting wood at the woodpile at dusk (night 1). Big and silent: a word at most, and a look.

lines.text: (A big lay brother at the woodpile, splitting logs in the rain. He stops with the axe on the block and looks at you.)
(Dunstan looks up from the block, then down again.)

answers.text: I'm Alric, the new porter. And you, brother?
Let me carry some of that for you.

lines.text: Dunstan.
(He sets the next log on the block.)
(He shakes his head. He looks at your hands a moment, then splits the log in one stroke.)
(The axe comes down behind you.)

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/edwin.talk.name: Brother Edwin
notes: Edwin, the novice, on the west walk at dusk (night 1), an armful of rushlights. The porter's friend; talks too fast.
The relic and the pilgrims (he never sees one leave); his novice's week; and, if the porter saw the shape
at the squint on night 0 (n0_squint_scare), the lane's horned demon, which had no horns.

lines.text: (A young brother hurries down the west walk with an armful of rushlights and nearly walks into you.)
Sorry! You're the porter. Alric? I'm Edwin, novice. Everyone's been talking about you. Well, Brother Osric has.
Is it true you came in through Aldgate on a cart? I've never been past Aldgate. I've never been past Cheapside.
You're back! I've still got all these to put out. Walk with me?

answers.text: Tell me about the relic.
What does a novice do all day?
Last night, through a squint, I saw something tall inside the wall.

lines.text: You haven't seen it? The saint's own finger, in a silver hand on the high altar. With the candles behind it, it glows.
Brother Ranulf won't let me near it. He says I breathe too hard.
Pilgrims come to it from Kent, from Essex. They pray, they sleep in the guesthouse, and they're gone before I'm up.
I've never once seen one leave. They're just not there.
Psalms. Psalms, and more psalms. I've forty by heart, and they tell me forty isn't a hundred and fifty.
And I'm reader at supper this week, up in the pulpit. So don't make me laugh. I mean it, Alric.
Inside our wall? At night? (He laughs, and then he doesn't.)
Tall? That's the lane's demon, with the horns. Jankin's been seeing it for years.
(You tell him it had no horns.)
No horns? (He's quiet a moment, which isn't like him.) Then I don't know what you saw.
See you at supper! Don't make me laugh!

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/godric.tal.name: Abbot Godric
notes: Abbot Godric in the chapter house at dusk (night 1), a blanket over his knees. Frail, kind, fatherly.
He welcomes the porter, blesses him, and speaks of the saint who keeps the house. He dreams badly (the drug; he doesn't know it).

lines.text: (The abbot sits on the stone bench of the chapter house with a blanket over his knees. He holds out a thin hand.)
Brother Alric. Come where I can see you. My eyes are better than Anselm's, but not by much in this light.
Welcome to our house. You're young. Good. The young sleep less and see more.
Still with an old man? The bell will ring for supper soon.

answers.text: Will you bless me, Father Abbot?
Tell me about the saint, Father Abbot.
What would you have of your porter, Father Abbot?

lines.text: (He lays his hand on your head. It's light and cold, and it shakes.)
The Lord keep your going out and your coming in. That's the porter's psalm. I chose it for you.
Our saint has kept this house since before London had a mayor. While the relic is on the altar, nothing evil comes in.
The pilgrims come to the bone, and the bone keeps us. That's how it has always been.
Lately I dream of the saint. (He looks toward the church, and doesn't finish.) Old men dream.
Keep the gate. Ring the bell. Count us in at Matins, every one.
And be kind at the grille. Half of London comes to a gate in the dark, and most of it is only cold.
God keep your going out, brother, and your coming in.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/hugh.talk.name: Prior Hugh
notes: Prior Hugh at dusk on the north walk (night 1). Cold; he suspects the new porter from the first.
He asks why a country house sent a boy to keep a London gate (n1_hugh_why), then gives his rule:
nobody comes in after the curfew bell without the prior (n1_hugh_rule).
Claims: n1_hugh_gate (true: he is investigating the deaths, and suspects the porter; his glare and jaw are how he tells the truth).
If the porter drank hard at the Keys he says so. hangover is cleared by the day-1 nap, so n0_saw_killing=drunk is the real test.

lines.text: (A tall brother stands in the middle of the north walk, hands in his sleeves, watching you come.)
The new porter. I am Hugh, prior of this house.
You came to us from the Cross Keys this morning smelling of it. I noticed. So did others.
A small house in the country sends a boy of nineteen to keep a gate in London. Why you?

answers.text: My abbot sent me, and I came.
There was no one else to send.
Why does it matter to you?

lines.text: Obedience. Keep some by you. You'll need it here.
That I believe.
Everything that comes in at that gate matters to me. You came in at it.

answers.text: Then we want the same thing, Father Prior.
Or is it only me you're watching?

lines.text: (He looks at you a long moment, as if he hadn't expected that.)
Then you'll not mind my watching it.
I've answered you, porter. I'll not answer twice.
Hear the one rule I care about. After the curfew bell, nobody comes in at that gate unless I say so.
Pilgrim, priest or the King's own uncle. You send for me, and you wait.
You've had your rule, porter. Go to your supper.
After the bell, porter. Remember.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/osric.talk.name: Brother Osric
notes: Osric, the cellarer, at the kitchen fire at dusk (night 1). Jolly; he feeds you. He promises extra bread at supper (n1_osric_bread).
If Thomas told the porter about the beast bled by the well (d1_asked_sand), he can ask Osric about it:
Osric backs the lie, and the cult notes the porter's curiosity (Suspicion +5, the wrong question to the wrong brother).
Claims: n1_osric_pig (lie: a man was killed by the well on night 0, and Osric started the killings; confront with window_killing).

lines.text: (A round brother at the kitchen fire, sleeves rolled, flour to the elbow. He beams at you.)
The porter! At last, a man with an honest appetite. I'm Osric, cellarer.
Everything you eat in this house goes through my hands.
Back again? Smell that. Patience, brother, patience.

answers.text: What's for supper, brother?
I slept through dinner.
I hear a beast was bled by the well last night.

lines.text: Pease pottage, with a little bacon in it for them that work nights. That's you.
And bread, our own, baked this morning. Rye from our own granary. Nothing bought in.
Slept through dinner? We can't have that. A porter who's hungry nods at his post.
I'll see you have the heel of the loaf at supper, and a second piece after. Eat it all, mind.
The pig? Aye, that was mine to do. I bled him by the well, where there's water to sluice the stones.

answers.text: A pig. I'll look for him in the pottage.
A pig, at midnight? In the rain?
I saw it from the Keys, brother. It was no pig.

lines.text: In the pottage, and the bacon in it. Every bit of him.
When else? Bleed a pig at Prime and he won't hang by Prime.
(He goes on kneading, and doesn't look up.)
(He laughs, a beat late.) Leave the kitchen's mess to the kitchen, brother, and I'll leave your gate to you.
(The smile comes too fast, and goes.)
From the Keys? In the rain, over a wall?
(He laughs, too loud.) A pig screams like a Christian when the knife goes in, brother. Ask any butcher in Eastcheap.
Come hungry! The bell won't be long!

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/ranulf.tal.name: Brother Ranulf
notes: Ranulf, the sacrist, at the candle stand in the nave at dusk (night 1). Dry, exact, never stops working.
He keeps the bells, the candles, the relic and the incense. He offers nothing yet (the remedy is night 3).
Hidden: he wears the horned costume; the relic is a pig's bone; the incense doses the choir.

lines.text: (The sacrist at the candle stand in the nave, trimming wicks with small shears. He doesn't stop.)
The porter. Ranulf, sacrist. The bell is mine. The ringing of it is yours. Don't be late with it.
Something else?

answers.text: What should I know about the candles?
Tell me about the relic.
What's the incense for?

lines.text: Wax on the altar, tallow everywhere else. Every one is counted.
If you find a lamp out on your round, light it from the sanctuary lamp and tell me. Not the prior. Me.
The saint's finger, in the silver hand on the altar. Pilgrims may kiss the glass.
I keep the key to it. Nobody opens it. Nobody needs to.
At Matins I cense the choir. Breathe it in. It's the prayers going up.
And it's good for the chest, in this damp.
The black ring, porter. Not after it.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/thomas.tal.name: Brother Thomas
notes: Thomas at dusk, at his herbs in the infirmary (night 1). Kind; he goes over the night's routine.
The killing seen from the Keys (n0_saw_killing): a dream, or the kitchen's beast being bled. Never the truth.
The guesthouse key: truthful, but he leaves locking to the porter and makes it sound unkind.
Anselm: an old man who frightens easily. If Anselm warned him on the tour, Thomas asks what he said.
Claims: n1_thomas_beast (lie: a man was killed by the well on night 0, not a beast; confront with window_killing).

lines.text: (Thomas at his bench, a mortar in his lap, grinding something that smells green. He smiles when he sees you.)
You slept. Good. The first night is the longest; after that your body learns it.
Supper at the bell, then the gate from Cole. Bar it. Matins at the black ring, then your round, then wait for Lauds.
Still here? The supper bell won't be long.

answers.text: Last night, from the Keys, I saw a man killed by the well.
What should I do with the guesthouse key?
How is Brother Anselm keeping?

lines.text: (He hears you out without stopping the pestle. Then he stops.)
You came to us this morning with Agnes's ale still in your eyes. At midnight, in rain, from the top of the Keys?
They bled a beast for the kitchen by the well last night. A lantern, a knife, a thing that kicks.
I'd have dreamed the same. But I'd not carry it to the abbot. He sleeps badly enough as it is.

answers.text: It was no beast, brother. I saw a man.
(Let it go.)

lines.text: From the top of the Keys you look down into our court, it's true. At midnight, in the rain, after a day on a cart.
The kitchen bled a beast by the well in the night, so it would hang by morning. A knife over a thing that kicks.
I can see how it looked. I'd not carry it to the abbot, though. He sleeps badly enough as it is.

answers.text: It was no beast, brother. I saw a man.
(Let it go.)

lines.text: (He sets the pestle down, and smiles at you.)
A beast, brother. I heard it from this bench, kicking and bawling. Nobody died in our court.

answers.text: Then I dreamed it.
You heard it? At midnight, through the rain?
I wrote it down that night. A man in a habit, dragging a man toward the cellar.

lines.text: Dreams come cheap in a strange bed. Put it by, brother.
Through the rain, and through a shut door. A pig makes himself heard.
(He takes up the pestle again, and says no more about it.)
(For a moment his face does nothing at all. Then the smile comes back, slower.)
You wrote it down.
Then write beside it that it was dark, and raining, and every brother here wears a black habit. So does the man who drags a pig to the cellar to hang.
Keep it on your ring with the gate's. Show a guest to his bed, and the rest is your judgement.
Anselm locked them in at night. Some guests took that ill, to be shut up like sheep.
Do as you think best. It's your gate now.
His eyes have gone white, both of them. I keep him here, where it's warm.
He frightens easily now, and he talks. Old porters' tales. Don't let him put them in your head.
Did he say something to you this morning, after I'd gone?

answers.text: He told me not to let them in after the bell.
He only wished me well.

lines.text: (He nods slowly, and goes back to his mortar.)
Don't let them in after the bell. Yes. He says it to the walls, most nights. Poor soul.
(He looks at you a moment longer than he needs to.)
Well. He likes you, then.
Eat well at supper, brother. You'll be glad of it by Matins.

game/chapters/night1/dialogue/warner.tal.name: Brother Bede
notes: Brother Bede, of the choir, under the eaves by the refectory door at dusk (night 1). Nervous; he keeps looking at the door.
He does NOT warn about the bread here: that is supper's scripted moment. He is only strange about supper.
He hangs in the bell tower on night 2: his stall, his climbs to be alone, the rooks that know him.

lines.text: (A thin brother under the eaves by the refectory door, his hood up. His eyes keep going past you to the door.)
You're the porter. I'm Bede. Choir, the third stall on the left. You'll count me at Matins.
(He's still watching the refectory door.)
Brother.

answers.text: What's for supper, brother?
What are you watching for, brother?
How do I ring Matins?

lines.text: Pottage. Bread. There's always bread.
(He lowers his voice.)
Eat slowly, brother. Watch what the rest of us leave.
Watching? (He makes himself look at you.) Nothing. I'm hungry, that's all. We're all hungry here.
The rope hangs at the foot of the tower. Pull, let it rise, pull again. Don't hold on when it rises.
I go up the tower stair sometimes, when I can't sleep. It's the one place in this house a man can think.
The rooks know me now. They don't even get up. Anyone else, they go up all at once.
God keep you, porter.

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/anselm.tal.name: Brother Anselm
notes: Anselm by the infirmary brazier at dusk (night 2). He heard the merchant carried past his door, or heard him leave cursing.
The knock with no one there frightens him more than anything; it's new to him. He hints at his guilt and won't tell.
Claims: n2_anselm_guests (hiding: he is blind now, but for years he let the victims in; pressed, he hints, and names no one).

lines.text: (Anselm in his chair by the brazier. He turns his face toward your step before you speak.)
They carried a man past my door this morning. Wet. I heard it run off him onto the flags.
(His voice drops.)
Did you lock the door, porter? I told you. I told you to.
I heard your merchant in the court this morning, cursing you for locking him in.
(He's nearly smiling.)
Let him curse. Let them all curse you, and go home.
The porter. You came through your first night. (He reaches for your hand, and holds it a moment.)
Still there? I can hear you breathing.

answers.text: Last night there was a knock at the gate, and no one there.
In your years at the gate, brother, did you ever lose a guest?

lines.text: (His hands find the arms of his chair and hold on.)
And nobody there. In thirty years at that gate I never had that.
Pray, porter. It's all I know to tell you.
(A long silence. His hands tighten on the arms of the chair.)
I'm blind, porter. I don't see anything now.
I don't see anything.

answers.text: Forgive me, brother. I shouldn't have asked.
You weren't blind then, brother.

lines.text: (He turns his face back to the brazier.)
No. You shouldn't.
(His mouth works a long while before anything comes out of it.)
Not every night. Some nights I didn't lock the door. Those mornings there was a bed empty by Lauds.
And I never asked whose. Never once. Don't make me say more.
Lock them in, porter.

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/choira.tal.name: Brother Wulfric
notes: Brother Wulfric on the south walk at dusk (night 2), rubbing his knees. Background; crabbed.
The drowned merchant, or the abbot's extra hour of prayer; the abbot has dreamed badly since Michaelmas.

lines.text: (Old Brother Wulfric on the south walk, rubbing his knees.)
A drunk drowns in our fishpond, and the abbot goes about with a face like he's seen the Devil.
In my day a drunk who drowned was a drunk who drowned.
The abbot had us on our knees an hour after chapter, praying for the house. My knees are older than his.
Still here, boy? Go and ring something.

answers.text: What is the abbot afraid of, brother?

lines.text: Bad dreams. He's had them since Michaelmas. At his age you dream of the grave, and he's earned it.
On the mark tonight, boy.

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/choirb.tal.name: Brother Aldo
notes: Brother Aldo in the nave at dusk (night 2), setting out the psalters in the stalls. Background.
Bede wasn't at Sext or None; nobody knows yet that he is dead (he's found when the porter rings Matins).
Aldo thinks he's up the tower sulking. Promising to count him in sets n2_choirb_bede.

lines.text: (Brother Aldo in the nave, setting out the psalters. At one stall he sets the book down, picks it up, sets it down.)
Have you seen Bede? He wasn't at Sext. Nor at None. The prior marked him.
He'll be up the tower with the rooks, sulking. He goes up there to think.
No Bede yet. He'll catch it from the prior.

answers.text: I'll look for him at Matins.

lines.text: Count him in for me, then. Third stall on the left.
If you see Bede, tell him the prior's asking.

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/choirc.tal.name: Brother Piers
notes: Brother Piers on the east walk at dusk (night 2), watching the rain. Background.
The drowned merchant (Thomas says drunk, so drunk it is), or the abbot's dreams and Bede off sulking.

lines.text: (Brother Piers on the east walk, watching the rain fill the garden beds.)
A man drowned in our fishpond. I'll not eat the carp this side of Easter.
Rain again. The cloister drain's choked. It'll be over our shoes by Matins.
Still raining.

answers.text: What are the brothers saying?

lines.text: That Thomas says he drowned drunk, so he drowned drunk. (He doesn't smile.) Thomas is never wrong about the dead.
That the abbot's dreaming badly, and Bede's gone off sulking again. Nothing new.
Keep dry, porter.

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/cole.talk.name: Cole
notes: Cole keeping the gate at dusk (night 2). Silent: a word or two at most, and a look.
If the merchant drowned, there's pond weed drying on his boots: he helped pull him out, or so it would seem.

lines.text: (Cole in the gate's arch, as he was last night. He looks at you a long moment.)
(There's green weed from the pond drying on his boots.)
(Cole looks at you and says nothing.)

answers.text: I'll take the gate after supper.
Did anyone come to the gate today?

lines.text: After supper.
(He shakes his head once.)
(Cole watches you go.)

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/dunstan.ta.name: Dunstan
notes: Dunstan at the woodpile at dusk (night 2), stacking logs out of the rain. Silent: a look, and no word at all tonight.

lines.text: (Dunstan at the woodpile, stacking split logs under the eaves out of the rain. He doesn't stop.)
(Dunstan doesn't look up.)

answers.text: (Pick up an armful and help him stack.)
Were you there when they pulled the merchant out, brother?

lines.text: (He watches you set the logs down. Then he lifts them off the pile and stacks them again, his own way.)
(He looks at you. Then he goes back to the logs.)
(Behind you, the logs go on thudding onto the pile.)

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/edwin.talk.name: Brother Edwin
notes: Edwin on the west walk at dusk (night 2). He opens on the night before: the drowned merchant (Osric carried him off),
the merchant who left cursing the lock, or just the porter's first night. Then the knock, the pardoner, and what
the brothers are saying: the abbot's bad dreams, and Ranulf on the incense. (The bread is night 3's talk.)

lines.text: (Edwin catches your sleeve the moment he sees you.)
Did you see him? The merchant, in the fishpond? I wasn't let look.
Brother Osric carried him off before Prime. He said a drowned man's no sight for a novice.
Your merchant went off this morning cursing you all the way to the gate! For locking him in!
I've never heard a man swear like it, and I've been to Billingsgate.
You're alive! I mean, of course you are. How was it? Was it long?
Brother Wulfric says the first night's the longest, and then they get longer.
Still here? Me too. I'm meant to be in the church.

answers.text: Last night there was a knock at the gate, and no one there.
I let a pardoner in last night.
What are the brothers saying today?

lines.text: And nobody there? (He's gone pale, and he's trying not to be.)
Boys from the lane. It'll have been boys. Won't it?
A pardoner! Did he have a feather from the Archangel's wing? They always have a feather.
Brother Hugh says pardoners are thieves with Latin. I'd still like to see the feather.
That Father Abbot had bad dreams. He told the chapter this morning, and asked us all to pray for the house.
Brother Hugh says it's the rain. Brother Ranulf says the incense isn't thick enough at Matins.
See you at supper! I'm reading again!

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/godric.tal.name: Abbot Godric
notes: Abbot Godric in the chapter house at dusk (night 2). Uneasy: he believes a demon troubles the house, but hasn't said so
to the chapter yet (he will at dawn, and order more incense). He dreams badly: the drug, though he doesn't know it.
He tells the porter to count every brother at Matins tonight, and to breathe the incense.

lines.text: (The abbot sits with his blanket in the chapter house, but he isn't reading. He's watching the door.)
Brother Alric. Come in, come in, and shut the door against the draught.
A guest of ours died in the night, in the water. I've said a mass for him, and I'll say another.
Your first night passed, and you're whole. Thank God for that.
You're still here, child? Good. I'd rather not sit alone tonight.

answers.text: What troubles you, Father Abbot?
Last night there was a knock at the gate, and no one there.
What would you have me do tonight, Father Abbot?

lines.text: Something has come into this house, brother. I feel it when I pray, like a draught from a door nobody opened.
I think it's a demon. I've not said so to the chapter. I'll not say it till I'm sure.
Last night I dreamed something knelt at the foot of my bed and counted on its fingers.
(He crosses himself.)
And no one there. If it comes again, don't open to it. Ring the bell and wake me.
Keep the gate. Count us at Matins, every one, and come to me if one is missing.
And breathe the incense, child. That's what it's for. I mean to have Ranulf burn more.
Count us all, brother. Every one.

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/hugh.talk.name: Prior Hugh
notes: Prior Hugh on the north walk at dusk (night 2). If the merchant died, he wants to know why the guesthouse was left
unlocked (n2_hugh_lock), and tells the porter the purse is gone (the merchant_purse note). He suspects the porter, and Walter.
Otherwise he is merely cold, and has a word on the pardoner. If Thomas told the porter the prior walks at night,
the porter can ask him why (n2_hugh_night): he turns it back on the porter.

lines.text: (The prior steps into your way on the walk, his wax tablet already open.)
You brought me the merchant this morning. The one thing you've done right.
Your round goes past the fishpond, porter. You saw nothing? Nothing at all?
You turned down the merchant's bed. This morning he was in the fishpond. Was the guesthouse locked, porter?

answers.text: No. I didn't think to lock it.
He was a guest, not a prisoner.
What are you saying I did?

lines.text: You didn't think. Anselm thought of it every night for thirty years.
A prisoner would be alive this morning.
I'm not saying. I'm asking. You'll know when I start saying.
He had a purse at your gate. You'll have seen it. There was none on him this morning.
Thomas says he drowned drunk. Drunk men drown with their purses on.
And you let the pardoner in after him. (He writes it on his tablet.) I'll be asking Walter about purses.
(The prior watches you come down the walk.)
You sent for me last night. (He looks almost surprised.) Good. That's the rule. Keep to it.
(The prior watches you come down the walk, and doesn't move out of your way.)
Porter. Your first night, and the house still standing. Don't let it go to your head.
You let the pardoner in. Walter sells pigs' knuckles to widows and calls them saints. Next time, send for me.
You turned the pardoner away. Good. Anselm let him in whenever he knocked.

answers.text: Why do you walk the abbey at night, Father Prior?

lines.text: (His face doesn't change, but he closes his tablet.)
Who told you that?
I walk where I please in this house. I'm its prior. Where do you walk, porter, between Matins and Lauds?
(He's writing on his tablet, and doesn't look up.)
Supper, porter.
We're not done, porter.

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/osric.talk.name: Brother Osric
notes: Osric at the kitchen fire at dusk (night 2). Jolly; he carried the drowned merchant (he handles the bodies).
He noticed whether the porter ate his bread last night (n1_ate_bread). Asking what's in the bread, once warned,
is the wrong question to the wrong brother (Suspicion +5), and ends the talk on his question.
Claims: n2_osric_rye (hiding: the rye is the abbey's own, and it carries the ergot the cult doses the house with).

lines.text: (Osric at the kitchen fire again, red-faced from it. He waves a ladle at you.)
A sad morning's work. I helped carry that merchant out of the pond, heavy as wet barley. Not kitchen talk.
You cleared your trencher last night! That's a porter I like.
You left your bread last night, brother. My bread! (He laughs, but his eyes stay on you.)
Tonight you'll eat it, or I'll know why.
Back for a taste? Not till the bell.

answers.text: What's for supper, brother?
What's in the bread, brother?

lines.text: Eels, stewed, if the eelman got through the rain. He did. And the bread, with a heel put by for you.
In my bread? Rye and salt and water and my own two hands. Rye from our own granary.

answers.text: Then I'll eat it, brother, and gladly.
Nothing else in it, brother? Nothing at all?

lines.text: That's the porter I like. The heel's put by for you, mind.
(He goes back to his kneading.)
(He keeps smiling. He has stopped kneading.)
Who's been talking to you about my bread, brother?
Come hungry, mind!

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/ranulf.tal.name: Brother Ranulf
notes: Ranulf on a ladder at the candle beam in the church at dusk (night 2). He keeps the bells.
Ringing Matins: the rope has been stiff with the wet and will feel heavy. (Tonight Bede hangs from it; Ranulf knows.)
If Ralph told the porter on night 0 how many candles the sacrist buys (n0_ralph_candles), the porter can say so:
the wrong question to the wrong brother (Suspicion +5).

lines.text: (Ranulf is up a ladder at the candle beam, fitting new candles. He looks down at you and doesn't come down.)
Porter.
You're in my light.

answers.text: Anything I should know about ringing Matins tonight?
Ralph the chandler says you buy twice the candles you used to.

lines.text: Pull like you mean it. The rope's been stiff with the wet these two nights. It'll feel heavy.
Ring the full peal. The abbot takes a short one for an omen, and he's had omens enough this week.
(He stops, a candle in each hand, and looks down at you a long moment.)
Ralph talks a great deal for a man who's paid on the nail.
A church in winter eats candles, porter. So does a house that prays more than it used to.
The full peal, porter.

game/chapters/night2/dialogue/thomas.tal.name: Brother Thomas
notes: Thomas at dusk, at his herbs in the infirmary (night 2). He opens, quietly, with the prior about the abbey at night
(n2_thomas_prior): true, and the prior is innocent. Then the merchant: drowned drunk (his lie), or alive, or turned away.
The knock with no one there: boys from the lane. Bede's warning about the bread: Bede fasts and sees things.
Telling him about the bread is the wrong brother (Suspicion +5). Bede is already dead; Thomas knows it.
Claims: n2_thomas_drowned (lie: no water in the lungs, rope marks on the wrists; confront with merchant_rope).

lines.text: (Thomas looks past you at the door before he speaks, and keeps his voice low.)
Brother. I've seen the prior about the abbey at night. In the court, by the guesthouse, long after Compline.
He has no business there at that hour. I don't say what it means. Only, if you see a man in the dark, it may be Hugh.
And the merchant. You did right to come to me this morning, and quietly. Ale and a fishpond: no fault of yours.

answers.text: He was sober at my gate, brother.
(Say nothing.)

lines.text: And the merchant. You took him to Hugh, I hear. He'll have made it your doing. It wasn't. The man was drunk.

answers.text: He was sober at my gate, brother.
(Say nothing.)

lines.text: And the merchant. Ale, and a fishpond in the dark. It's no fault of yours, brother. Don't carry him.

answers.text: He was sober at my gate, brother.
(Say nothing.)

lines.text: (He sets the pestle down.)
I pressed the pond out of his chest with my own hands, brother. He drowned. Drink and the dark, nothing more.

answers.text: God rest him, then.
A man who stood so steady at my gate?
Then who tied his hands? There were rope marks on his wrists.

lines.text: God rest him. Say his name at Matins, if you like. It does the living good.
Steady men drink too, brother. I've laid out enough of them to know.
(He takes up the pestle again.)
(The pestle stops. For a moment his face is a stranger's.)
Rope marks.
They drew him out with a rope, brother, and Dunstan with his boathook. A drowned man's skin marks like wet clay.
You've a sharp eye. Keep it on your gate.
Your merchant left at first light, cursing the porter who locked him in like a sheep. Well. He's alive to curse.
You turned the merchant away. We receive every guest as Christ, the Rule says. Still, it was your first night.
(Thomas is back at his mortar.)
Brother. Supper soon.

answers.text: What would the prior be doing out at night?
Last night there was a knock at the gate, and no one there.
Someone warned me not to eat the bread.

lines.text: I don't know, and I'd rather not guess at a brother's sins.
You're up all night. You'll see more than I do. Watch, that's all I ask.
(For a moment he doesn't answer. Then he smiles.)
Boys from the lane, knocking and running. They did it to Anselm for years.
And Mab sleeps more than she lets on. Don't lose sleep over a knock.
Bede, was it? I saw him at your ear.
Bede fasts till he faints, and then he sees things in the rafters. Eat your bread, brother. You need your strength.
Keep it between us, brother. About the prior.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/anselm.tal.name: Brother Anselm
notes: Anselm at dusk, in the infirmary (night 3). The old porter, blind, hunched in his chair, his stick across his knees.
Guilty and terrified: he let victims in for years. He won't say so, and nothing here says so.

lines.text: (The old man in the chair turns his face to the door before you reach it.)
That's the porter's step. You walk like a man who's been told not to run.
Still with us, then. Good. Sit, if you like.
(His milky eyes settle on a place just beside your face.)
Back again? Nobody else comes twice. Sit.

answers.text: What did you mean, don't let them in after the bell?
Tell me about keeping the gate, brother.
How did your eyes go, Brother Anselm?

lines.text: (His hand finds your sleeve and grips it. He listens to the room before he speaks.)
I meant what I said. No more than that.
Bar it at the bell and keep it barred. Whoever knocks. Whatever they tell you.
Don't ask me why, boy. I'm old, and I can't see who's listening.
Thirty years I kept it. I knew every knock in the ward by the sound.
The carter's, the bailiff's, Walter's. Pilgrims knock soft, as if the gate might bite.
I let in whoever came. That was the rule I was given, and I kept it.
(He's quiet a while.)
Write them all down, boy. Every one. Somebody should.
They went like milk in a pail. Grey at the edges first, then the middle. Two winters.
I hear better than I did. That's the bargain God makes with you.
The night before last, I heard the tower creak before ever you rang. There was no wind. Only the rain.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/carter.tal.name: the carter
notes: The carter in the lane at dusk (night 3), walking his empty wagon home before dark. A line or two, and he's gone.
Night 3 keeps its own; the other nights are game/chapters/common/lane/carter.talk.

lines.text: (The carter, walking at his horse's head, the wagon rattling empty behind him.)
Porter. I can't stop. I want to be out through Aldgate before they shut it.

answers.text: How's the lane tonight?
Have you seen any pilgrims on the road?
Good night. Go carefully.

lines.text: Quiet as a church. Quieter than your church, by what they say.
Hob's doing no trade. Nobody wants to drink with your wall looking at them.
Not one, all day, from Mile End in. Last week I'd pass a dozen, with their staffs and their badges.
Word gets about, porter. Folk would sooner walk to Canterbury.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/choir_brot.name: A choir brother
notes: The choir brothers at dusk (night 3); Wulfric, Aldo and Piers all share this, so nobody is named.
Faces you know from Matins. Not in the cult. Bede, who warned you about the bread, sang beside them.

lines.text: (A brother of the choir, his hands in his sleeves. You know his face from Matins.)
Porter. God give you good evening.

answers.text: Did you know the brother who died?
The brother who died warned me off the bread. Why?
Good night, brother.

lines.text: Bede. Nine years I sang beside him at the night office. He sang flat, and knew it, and sang anyway.
The abbot says the demon took him. Maybe so.
He was frightened, those last days. But not of demons. Bede laughed at demons.
(He looks toward the kitchen before he answers.)
He told you that too? He'd stopped eating it. He hid it in his sleeve and threw it over the wall.
I asked him why. He said it was better I didn't know. Then he was dead.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/cole.talk.name: Cole
notes: Cole at dusk, keeping the gate (night 3). Lay brothers don't talk (Look and Feel, "Characters").

lines.text: (Cole stands in the open gateway, arms folded, watching the lane. He looks round at you and says nothing.)

answers.text: Did anyone come to the gate today, Brother Cole?
I'll take the gate after supper, brother.
Good evening, Brother Cole.

lines.text: (Cole looks at you, then back at the lane. He says nothing.)
(He says nothing. He looks at you a moment longer than he needs to, then back at the lane.)

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/dunstan.ta.name: Dunstan
notes: Dunstan at dusk, by the woodpile (night 3). Lay brothers don't talk (Look and Feel, "Characters").

lines.text: (Dunstan rests his axe on the block and looks at you. He says nothing.)

answers.text: Is there wood enough for the winter, brother?
Have you seen anything strange, Brother Dunstan?
Good night, Brother Dunstan.

lines.text: (Dunstan looks up from the woodpile. He says nothing.)
(He says nothing. He sets a log on the block, and the axe comes down.)

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/edwin.talk.name: Brother Edwin
notes: Edwin at dusk, on the west walk (night 3). The novice, your friend: gangly, freckled, a book under his arm. He talks too fast.
He's frightened and trying not to show it. (He dies on night 4. Nothing here says so.)

lines.text: (Edwin is pacing the west walk, his book shut under his arm. His face lights up when he sees you.)
Alric! There you are. I looked for you at None, then I remembered you sleep all day. You lucky man.
You again! Good. Stay a bit. The walk's very long when there's nobody on it.

answers.text: How are you, Edwin?
The brother who died warned me off the bread.
Did you know the brother in the bell tower?

lines.text: Me? Well. I'm well. I'm not sleeping, but nobody's sleeping. Except Brother Wulfric. He'd sleep through Doomsday.
I keep reading the same page. Look. It's the same psalm. I've been on it since Martinmas.
(He laughs, too quickly.)
Bede said that? To you? He never said a word to me, and I sat by him at table a whole year.
It's only bread. I've eaten it since I was twelve.
(He thinks about it, and the grin goes.)
I'll leave mine tonight, if you leave yours. We'll be hungry together. That's nearly a feast.
They're saying you found him. When you rang the bell. Is it true?
Bede taught me my letters. He'd rap my knuckles with a rule, and then give me an apple after.
Father Abbot says the demon did it. I'd rather it was the demon, Alric. Isn't that a terrible thing to want?
I'll see you at supper! Sit by me, if they let you.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/godric.tal.name: Abbot Godric
notes: Abbot Godric at dusk, in the chapter house (night 3). Small, frail, very old and kind; he leans on his crosier and coughs.
Not in the cult. Drugged hardest, he believes the demon has come, and has ordered more incense to drive it out.

lines.text: (The abbot sits alone on the stone bench, both hands on his crosier. The air in here is blue with incense.)
Come in, my son. Let an old man look at you. You've lost colour since you came to us.
(The abbot coughs into his sleeve for a long while before he can speak.)
Forgive me. The smoke. A small price for the safety of the house.

answers.text: Is there truly a demon in the house, Father Abbot?
How am I doing as porter, Father Abbot?
Will you bless me, Father Abbot?

lines.text: It has come into our house. I said so before the brothers this morning, and I'll say it again.
I have felt it at the night office, my son. The way you feel a draught from a door left open.
So we'll smoke it out. Incense at every office, and prayer. Our saint will not suffer it long.
Thomas tells me you keep good hours, and you ring the bell well. That's most of it.
The prior is harder to please. He's no harder on you than he is on himself. Bear with him.
Anselm kept that gate thirty years. Be patient with yourself. It took him a while too.
(You kneel. His hand on your head is as light as paper, and it shakes.)
The Lord bless you and keep you, and keep the gate through you. Go in peace, my son.
(He signs the cross over you, and coughs.)

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/hugh.talk.name: Prior Hugh
notes: Prior Hugh at dusk, on the north walk (night 3). Lean, upright, a scarred jaw; he writes everything on his wax tablet.
Harsh, and he suspects the new porter. He asked at dawn where he was in the night; now he asks again. (He's looking into the deaths. Nothing here says so.)
Claims: n3_hugh_night (true): he wants to know who walks the house at night. He's investigating the deaths.

lines.text: (The prior steps out from behind a pillar into your path, his wax tablet open in his hand.)
Porter. This morning I asked you where you were in the night. I'll ask again.
A man who tells the truth tells it the same way twice. Where were you?

answers.text: I'll tell you what I saw, Father Prior.
I was at the gate, Father Prior.
What do you want with me, Father Prior?

lines.text: (The prior writes on his wax tablet and doesn't look up.)
I've nothing more for you, porter. Go to your supper.
(You tell him what you saw in the night: the rope, what fell past you, the rest.)
(He writes it all on the wax. Behind you, in the church, a door closes softly.)
Tell no one else what you've told me. No one. Now go.
At the gate. All night, at the gate. And yet you were in the tower when Bede came down, and nobody else was.
The porter is first to everything, it seems.
(He writes one word on the wax, and steps aside to let you pass.)
I want to know who walks this house at night. Since you came to that gate, a brother has hanged in our tower.

answers.text: Then we want the same thing, Father Prior.
You walk it at night yourself, Father Prior. Who watches you?

lines.text: (He looks at you a long moment. Then he writes something on the wax.)
Then keep your eyes open on that gate, and bring what you see to me. Not to the abbot. To me.
I'm not a fool, porter, whatever the abbot believes. Go to your supper. I'll be watching you at it.
I am prior of this house. I walk where I please, and I answer to the abbot, not the porter.
I'm not a fool, porter, whatever the abbot believes. Go to your supper. I'll be watching you at it.
Walk away, then. I'll write that down too.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/lane_woman.name: Margery
notes: Margery in the lane at dusk (night 3), her basket on her arm, hurrying home before dark.
Night 3 keeps its own; the other nights are game/chapters/common/lane/margery.talk. She names herself, in case he never met her.

lines.text: (A woman with a covered basket on her arm, walking fast.)
Margery, brother, from by Saint Andrew's, if you've forgotten. I'm not stopping. Not this week.

answers.text: Where are you off to in such a hurry, Margery?
What does the lane say about the abbey?
Good night, Margery.

lines.text: Home, where else? Before Gib lights the lanterns, with the door barred and the shutters too.
My husband laughs at me for it. He can laugh from behind a barred door.
That a holy brother hanged himself in your bell tower. Or the devil hanged him, your abbot says.
Devil or rope, brother, he's dead all the same. And I'm late.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/mab.talk.name: Mab
notes: Mab at the gate (night 3), from dusk until the knocks. She sees who comes and goes, nobody asks her, and she never eats the abbey's bread.
Night 3 keeps its own; the other nights are game/chapters/common/lane/mab.talk. Alms once (n3_mab_alms): a heel of Fenchurch Street bread.

lines.text: (Mab sits against the wall by the gate, her clapper in her lap, her face wrapped to the eyes.)
Porter. You look worse every night. I say it kindly.
(She knocks her clapper once against the stones.)
Still here? So am I.

answers.text: What have you seen, Mab?
Do you eat the abbey's bread, Mab?
(Give her alms.)

lines.text: Everyone who goes in at that gate, and everyone who comes out. Nobody asks me.
Last night something walked the lane after the bell. Taller than a man. It came from the corner of your wall.
And the rooks came off your tower before Matins, all at once, screaming. Before your bell, porter. Not after.
Theirs? Never. Not a crumb in eleven years, and I've been hungry enough to eat straw.
Somebody's told you something about it. I can see it on you.
Good. Then I don't have to.
(You drop a coin in the bowl at her feet.)
God keep you, porter. Here. It's not theirs. A baker on Fenchurch Street makes it.
(She sets a heel of bread on the step between you, wrapped in a cloth, and draws back.)

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/osric.talk.name: Brother Osric
notes: Osric at dusk, in the kitchen (night 3). The cellarer: short and heavy, round red face, always smiling; his ring of keys jingles.
Jolly; he feeds you extra bread. (He started the killings. Nothing here says so.)
Claims: n3_osric_page (lie): the cats get at the ledger. The cult tore the page (night 2); Osric handles the bodies.

lines.text: (Osric is at the kitchen fire, sleeves rolled, his ring of keys swinging at his belt. His face is red from the heat.)
The porter! Come in out of the cold. Mind the pot. You look half starved.
Back again? You can smell supper, can you. Not yet, porter. Not yet.

answers.text: What goes into the bread, Brother Osric?
What's for supper, brother?
Has anyone been at my ledger, Brother Osric?

lines.text: My bread? Rye from our own granary, baked in our own oven. Best in the ward.
There's a bitter crust on it this week. The rye came in damp. It does no harm.
(He laughs, and claps you on the shoulder with a floury hand.)
I'll keep the heel back for you. A growing lad wants the heel.
Pease pottage, rye bread and small ale. Same as last night, and the night before.
Father Abbot looks to me like a man about to order a fast. Eat while you can, porter.
Your ledger? Who'd want it? A list of wet pilgrims and their boots.
(He's still smiling. The knife in his hand has stopped.)
Keep your cell door shut, porter. The cats get in. A cat will eat anything.

answers.text: I'll keep it shut, brother.
Cats, brother? I never said anything was gone.
A page is gone, brother. And a bed in the guesthouse stands empty that I wrote full.

lines.text: Good lad. Now out of my kitchen, before you put your elbow in the pot.
(He laughs.) Didn't you? You've the face of a man who's lost something. Mind the pot, porter.
(He turns back to his fire.)
(The smile goes out of his face. Then it's back, too wide.)
Then your pilgrim got up early and went on his way, and took his page for a keepsake.
Count your beds, porter. I count loaves.
Don't be late for supper! I'll keep the heel back for you.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/ranulf.tal.name: Brother Ranulf
notes: Ranulf at dusk, in the church (night 3). The sacrist: rigid, a narrow pale face that doesn't blink; his censer chain clinks.
He keeps the relic, the candles and the incense. (He wears the horned costume. Nothing here says so.)

lines.text: (Ranulf is trimming the candles along the choir, one by one. He doesn't turn until you're close.)
Porter. You're early. The church isn't yours until Matins.
(He goes on trimming the candles. The censer hangs from his belt on its chain.)
Porter. Again.

answers.text: Why so much incense, Brother Ranulf?
What is the relic, brother?
