You burn a great many candles now, brother.

lines.text: Father Abbot has ordered it at every office now. Twice the measure at Matins.
The smoke drives out what shouldn't be here. Breathe it in, porter. Breathe deep. It's for your protection.
The saint's finger, in its silver case. Pilgrims walk from Kent to kiss the glass over it.
It's in my keeping. Not yours. Not the prior's. Mine.
Wax is dear, and the house burns more of it every night. Father Abbot wants no dark corner for the thing to stand in.
(He doesn't blink.)
Don't take my candles to light your lantern, porter. I count them.

game/chapters/night3/dialogue/thomas.tal.name: Brother Thomas
notes: Thomas at dusk, in the infirmary (night 3). Tall, thin, stooped, gentle deep-set eyes, fingers stained from his herbs; he hums at his mortar.
Your first ally. He tells you what he has noticed, always about someone else. (He leads the cult. Nothing here says so.)
At supper Ranulf offers his remedy and Thomas warns you off it; the headaches answer sets that up.
Claims: n3_thomas_prior (misleading): the prior was up the tower stair first, which is so; he says it to point at an innocent man. Pressing is the right read.

lines.text: (Thomas is at his bench, grinding something in a mortar and humming. He stops when he sees you, and smiles.)
Alric. Come in. You slept, I hope? You've the look of a man who dreamed.
(Thomas looks up from his mortar. His fingers are stained green to the knuckle.)
Back again? Sit. I'm only grinding.

answers.text: My head aches, Brother Thomas. It won't let up.
How is Brother Anselm?
Did you know the brother in the bell tower?

lines.text: Behind the eyes? Worse when you wake?
(He tilts your face to the window and looks into one eye, then the other.)
It's the night hours. A body takes a month to learn them. Sleep with your shutter closed, and eat.
And if anyone offers you physic for it, come to me first. Physic is my trade.
Quieter since the tower. He asks after you. Old porters never stop keeping the gate.
Don't let him frighten you, Alric. His mind wanders at night. He hears things.
Bede. I'm sorry you were the one who found him. A hard thing, on your second night.
Father Abbot says the demon. I've seen what I've seen in this house. I don't argue with him.
Only I wonder about the prior. He was up the tower stair before any of us. Quick, for a man woken by a bell.

answers.text: Then I'll watch him, brother.
Before any of you? Who saw him go up?

lines.text: Quietly, Alric. Watch, and say nothing to him. He's the prior, and you're the porter.
I say only what I saw. Make of it what you like.
(He takes up his pestle again.)
Rest before supper, Alric. The nights are long.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/anselm.tal.name: Brother Anselm
notes: Anselm at dusk, in his chair in the infirmary (night 4, fog). Blind, guilty and terrified. He hears men on the night stair
and says his beads. On copied keys (keys_copied) he gives the night-4 rule sideways: bar from inside, a bar has no key.
If Thomas has named Simon (n4_thomas_simon), Anselm says there's no harm in Simon, and stops himself.

lines.text: (Anselm in his chair. The fog has got into the infirmary and hangs about the brazier.)
Fog. I can smell it. Wet stone and the river. A man could walk right past you in it.
(His milky eyes settle on a place just beside your face.)
Back again, porter? Sit.

answers.text: What do you hear at night, Brother Anselm?
Someone has copied my keys, brother.
What do you know of Brother Simon?

lines.text: Feet on the night stair, after Compline, when every brother's abed. More than one pair.
They walk alike. Like men who've walked together a long while.
I lie still, and I say my beads, and I don't call out. God forgive me, I never call out.
(He laughs, with nothing in it.)
Copied. There were always more keys to that gate than there were porters, boy.
If you've a guest you want to keep, tell him to bar his door from inside. A bar has no key.
Simon? He brings me my broth when Thomas is busy. He talks to me about his mother in Kent.
There's no harm in Simon. Whoever told you different, ask yourself why they...
(He stops, and turns his face to the wall.)
Bar it at the bell, porter.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/choira.tal.name: Brother Wulfric
notes: Brother Wulfric on the south walk at dusk (night 4, fog), rubbing his knees. The oldest of the choir; crabbed.
His last talk: ordinary, and a little sad. (He is killed in the fog on the round tonight. Nothing here says so.)

lines.text: (Old Brother Wulfric on the south walk, a shape in the fog until you're close. He's rubbing his knees.)
Fog. My knees had it before the bell this morning. Forty years, and they've never once been wrong.
Still here, boy? Go and ring something.

answers.text: How are you bearing the fast, brother?
How did you come to the abbey, brother?

lines.text: Better than the young ones. I've kept every Lent since before you were born. An empty belly's a quiet one.
(His stomach growls. He ignores it.)
My mother walked me to that gate when I was eleven, with a cheese for the cellarer.
Anselm let us in. He had both his eyes then.
I've not been past Aldgate since. I meant to see the sea again, once, before the end.
Well. There's time yet.
On the mark tonight, boy. Don't keep my knees waiting.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/choirb.tal.name: Brother Aldo
notes: Brother Aldo in the nave at dusk (night 4, fog), setting out the psalters. Background; young.
Bede's stall stays empty by the abbot's order. If Thomas has named Simon (n4_thomas_simon), Aldo bears it out:
Simon sleeps in the next bed and goes down the night stair after Compline (because Thomas sends him).

lines.text: (Brother Aldo in the nave, setting out the psalters. The fog has come in at the west door and hides the altar.)
Porter. Mind where you walk. I've lost two psalters in it already.
Still here? So am I. There's no supper to go to.

answers.text: Why is Brother Bede's stall left empty?
What do you know of Brother Simon?

lines.text: Father Abbot says nobody's to sit in it. His psalter's still there. Nobody will touch it.
Nobody will sit next to it either. So I do.
Simon? His bed's next to mine. He's up after Compline, these last nights. I hear him go down the night stair.
He says he can't sleep. Who can?
Ring it loud tonight, porter. We'll want to hear it through this.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/choirc.tal.name: Brother Piers
notes: Brother Piers on the east walk at dusk (night 4, fog). Background; dry.
What the brothers say: the abbot's visitor, and the fast to starve it. If Thomas has named Simon (n4_thomas_simon):
Thomas nursed Simon through a fever at Michaelmas, and Simon would do anything Thomas told him.

lines.text: (Brother Piers on the east walk, watching the fog fill the garth like milk in a bowl.)
You can't see the far walk. I keep thinking someone's standing in it.
Still foggy.

answers.text: What are the brothers saying?
What do you know of Brother Simon?

lines.text: That the abbot saw it at the foot of his bed. That it's hungry, and we fast so it finds nothing in us to eat.
(He doesn't smile.)
I'd sooner eat.
Simon keeps to himself. Thomas nursed him through a fever at Michaelmas, and he's been Thomas's shadow since.
He'd walk into the river if Thomas told him it was good for his chest.
Mind the fog, porter.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/cole.talk.name: Cole
notes: Cole at dusk, keeping the gate (night 4, fog). Lay brothers don't talk (Look and Feel, "Characters").

lines.text: (Cole stands in the open gateway. Behind him the fog has swallowed the lane. He looks round at you and says nothing.)

answers.text: Did anyone come to the gate today?
I'll take the gate at the bell.
Good evening, Brother Cole.

lines.text: (Cole looks at you, then back at the fog. He says nothing.)
(He says nothing. He looks at you a moment longer than he needs to, then back into the fog.)

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/dunstan.ta.name: Dunstan
notes: Dunstan at dusk, by the woodpile (night 4, fog). Lay brothers don't talk (Look and Feel, "Characters").

lines.text: (You hear the axe before you see him: Dunstan, splitting logs in the fog. He stops and looks at you. He says nothing.)

answers.text: Have you seen anyone about, brother?
Will the fog lift by Matins, do you think?
Good night, Brother Dunstan.

lines.text: (Dunstan looks up from the block. He says nothing.)
(He says nothing. He sets a log on the block and looks at you over it until you look away.)

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/edwin.talk.name: Brother Edwin
notes: Edwin at dusk, on the west walk (night 4, fog). He has seen the demon's face; the dusk scene has him whisper it, and
that he'll tell after Matins. Here he's jumpy and won't say more: after Matins, he swears it. (He dies before Matins.
Nothing here says so.) The lines work whether or not the whisper has come yet.

lines.text: (Edwin on the west walk, his book hugged to his chest. He jumps when you come out of the fog, then laughs too loudly.)
Alric! Don't come up on a man like that. Not in this.
(Edwin hasn't moved. He's watching the fog at the end of the walk.)
Still here? Good. Stay a bit.

answers.text: What has frightened you, Edwin?
How are you bearing the fast?
What are you reading?

lines.text: (He looks over your shoulder into the fog before he answers.)
Not here. Not now. After Matins, I swear it. I'll come to your gate and tell you everything.
Somebody's always listening in this house, Alric. Even in the fog. Especially in the fog.
I left my bread last night, like we said. And now there's none to leave. I'm so hungry I could eat my book.
No supper! I'm so hungry I could eat my book. Psalms and all.
The same as ever. Psalm ninety, the one we sing at Compline. You shall not fear the terror of the night.
I've said it a hundred times since None. It isn't working.
After Matins, Alric. At your gate. Don't forget.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/godric.tal.name: Abbot Godric
notes: Abbot Godric at dusk, in the chapter house (night 4, fog). He has ordered the house to fast and doubled the incense again.
Frail, pious and frightened; drugged hardest, he believes. Telling him about the crypt: he'll send Ranulf down to
bless it, so the cult hears of it (Suspicion +5).

lines.text: (The chapter house is thick with smoke. The abbot sits in his blanket, a psalter open on his knees, not reading it.)
My son. Forgive us, there's no supper tonight. I've ordered the house to fast until it leaves us.
(The abbot coughs into his sleeve for a long while.)
Sit, child. Sit with me a little. I'd rather not be alone in here.

answers.text: Why have you ordered the fast, Father Abbot?
What have you seen, Father Abbot?
I saw a bound man killed at the altar in the crypt.

lines.text: Our Lord said some kinds go out only by prayer and fasting. So we'll pray, and we'll fast.
And Ranulf will burn twice what he burned. It shall find nothing in this house to feed on.
(He looks at the door before he answers.)
It came again last night, to the foot of my bed, and counted.
It had a brother's face, I think. I couldn't tell you whose.
Pray for me, child. I'm too old to be this afraid.
(His hand finds his crosier and holds it.)
Under the saint's own altar? Then it's in the crypt with our saint. God help us.
I'll have Ranulf go down tonight and bless every stone of it. Ranulf will know what to do.
Pray, my son. Pray and fast. It can't abide either.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/hugh.talk.name: Prior Hugh
notes: Prior Hugh at dusk, on the north walk (night 4, fog). Cold; he's investigating. He heard two men run the cloister
after Matins last night and wants to know what the porter saw. If the porter has told him the truth before
(n3_told_prior, or everything at night 2's dawn), he says so. Telling him about the crypt: Suspicion +10 (Ranulf overhears).
If the keys were copied (keys_copied), he looks at them and finds the wax: where were they? (n4_hugh_keys)

lines.text: (The prior comes out of the fog so close you nearly walk into him. His wax tablet is already open.)
Porter. Two men ran the cloister last night after Matins, one behind the other. I heard them from this walk.
The first of them was you.
You've told me the truth before, and I wrote it down. Do it again.
What did you see?

answers.text: I saw a bound man killed at the altar in the crypt.
It was the demon, Father Prior.
It wasn't me, Father Prior. I was never there.

lines.text: (You tell him: the light, the bound man, the figure at the altar. He writes it all on the wax.)
(Somewhere in the fog behind you, a door closes softly.)
Under the saint's altar. Tell no one else. Not the abbot. Not anyone.
The demon. The abbot's word for it.
Whatever ran behind you was out of breath, porter. I heard it. Demons don't pant.
Then someone wears your face. I'll find out who.
Your keys. Give them here.
(He turns them in the grey light and scrapes a tooth with his thumbnail. Wax comes away.)
Someone has taken a mould of these. When were they out of your hands?

answers.text: I was in the infirmary last night, with Brother Thomas.
I don't know, Father Prior.
They've never left me, Father Prior.

lines.text: With Thomas. All night, and your keys on your belt the whole while.
(He writes one word on the wax, and gives the keys back.)
A lock two men have a key to is no lock, porter. Remember that tonight.
You don't know. The porter, and he doesn't know where his keys go at night.
A lock two men have a key to is no lock. Remember that tonight.
Then the wax grew on them by itself. (He drops them in your hand.)
A lock two men have a key to is no lock, porter. Remember that tonight.
(The prior is a dark shape in the fog, writing.)
Go, porter. And keep your keys on you.
I'll find you, porter. In fog or out of it.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/osric.talk.name: Brother Osric
notes: Osric at dusk, locking the kitchen door (night 4, fog). The abbot's fast: no supper, the refectory locked.
Jolly as ever. (Tonight his mask comes off in the chase. Nothing here says so.)
Who could copy a key, and the bakehouse oven: the wrong questions to the wrong brother (Suspicion +5 each).

lines.text: (Osric is locking the kitchen door, his ring of keys in his fist. He turns round beaming.)
The porter! You've come for your supper, and there's none. Father Abbot's fast. I've locked my own kitchen.
Still here? There's nothing behind that door but cold pots, porter. I promise you.

answers.text: How long will the fast last, brother?
Who in this house could copy a key, brother?
When was the bakehouse oven last lit?

lines.text: Not a crumb till it leaves us, Father Abbot says, so it finds nothing in us to feed on.
(He pats his belly and laughs.)
I've stores enough to last me. It's you I worry for. Skin and bone, and up all night.
(The keys in his fist go quiet.)
Copy a key? Whatever for?
I've forty keys on this ring, porter, and I've never once needed a copy of one.
Every morning, for the bread. Not today, with the fast. It's as cold as a grave in there.
(He's still smiling.)
Why? Were you thinking of climbing in?
Pray hard, porter! It's all there is tonight!

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/ranulf.tal.name: Brother Ranulf
notes: Ranulf at dusk, filling the censers in the choir (night 4, fog). Smooth. (He wears the horned costume. Nothing here says so.)
The abbot has doubled the incense again; Ranulf wants the porter in the choir at Matins, not by the door (from night 4
the door is where a man can keep out of the smoke). His remedy: taken (n3_took_remedy) or refused (n3_refused_remedy).
Asking what is kept in the crypt is the wrong question to the wrong brother (Suspicion +10): he knows who ran last night.
Claims: n4_ranulf_crypt (lie): the light below is candles for the dead. The cult lights one for each soul fed to the rite.

lines.text: (Ranulf is filling the censers in the choir from a leather bag. The fog has come in at the west door.)
Porter. Mind the step. You can't see the floor tonight.
(He goes on filling the censers. The chain clinks.)
Porter. Again.

answers.text: Why so much incense, brother?
What is in your remedy, brother?
What is kept in the crypt, brother?

lines.text: Father Abbot has doubled it again. Four times what we burned at Martinmas.
And your place at Matins is in the choir with us, porter. Not back by the door, where the smoke doesn't reach.
Did it ease your head? It will, given time. I'll mix you another whenever you like.
You've only to ask me. Not Thomas. Me.
You wouldn't take it last night. Thomas had a word in your ear. I saw. Thomas has a word for everyone.
Your head will get worse, porter. Come to me when it does.
For your headaches. A little poppy, a little honey, nothing more. Come to me after Matins, if your head is bad.
(The censer stops halfway to its hook.)
The saint's bones, and the old abbots under them. The stair is kept locked. It's no part of your round.
If you see a light below, porter, it's mine. I keep candles burning for the dead.

answers.text: God rest them, then.
Candles for abbots two hundred years dead, brother? Every night?
I found a page by the altar below. Ten candles in a ring, and a soul for each.

lines.text: Amen. Keep to your round, porter, and leave the dead to me.
Every night. The dead are owed their light. That is the sacrist's business, not the porter's.
(He hangs the censer, and turns his back on you.)
(The chain goes still in his hand. His eyes go to the altar steps, and come back.)
Old books are full of old foolishness. Whatever you picked up down there, it belongs to the church.
Bring it to me, porter. Don't show it about.
In the choir, porter. Not by the door.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/simon.talk.name: Brother Simon
notes: Brother Simon at dusk, in the cloister garth on the low wall of the herb beds (night 4, fog). A quiet choir brother; nervous.
Not in the cult. Thomas has sent him to do a dirty job tonight (scrubbing blood) and he can't say so.
If Thomas has named him (n4_thomas_simon), the porter can ask where he goes at night (trust -5: he takes it badly).
Telling him to keep to the dormitory is a warning ([warn]); he takes it badly, and he trusts Thomas more than the porter.
Claims: n4_simon_night (hiding): he can't sleep, he walks. True, but Thomas sends him out at night; pressed, he says he's bid, not by whom.

lines.text: (A thin brother on the wall of the herb beds, picking at a thread on his sleeve. He stands too fast when he sees you.)
Porter. I was only taking the air. There's not much else to take tonight.
(Simon is back on the wall, picking at the same thread.)
Porter.

answers.text: Where do you go at night, brother?
How are you keeping, brother?
Keep to the dormitory tonight, brother. Bar the door.

lines.text: (The thread snaps in his fingers.)
Who says I go anywhere? I can't sleep. I walk. Is that a sin now, with all the rest?

answers.text: No sin, brother. I can't sleep either.
Walk where, brother? Alone, at that hour?

lines.text: (He looks toward the infirmary, then at the ground.)
No. No sin. Leave me be, porter.
(He looks toward the infirmary, then at the ground.)
I go where I'm bid, porter. I do what I'm told, and I don't ask. I'm not to talk of it.
Don't ask me again. Please.
Hungry. Cold. Afraid, like everyone.
I came here to sing, porter. It's all I'm good for. I wish they'd let me only sing.
(He goes white.)
Why would you say that to me? Who told you to say it?
I'll go where I'm bid. I'm a brother of this house, not a guest you can lock in.
Don't tell anyone you said that to me. Please.
God keep you, porter.

game/chapters/night4/dialogue/thomas.tal.name: Brother Thomas
notes: Thomas at dusk, at his mortar in the infirmary (night 4, fog; the house fasts, no supper).
If he hid the porter from the hunter last night (n3_thomas_hid_you), he gives him a story for it: he was here, for his head.
Brother Simon out at night: he says it first (n4_thomas_simon) unless the porter has already heard it from him tonight
(the dusk scene should set the same flag), then comes back to it. True, and it costs him nothing: he sends Simon out.
Telling him about the crypt is reporting it the safe way (trust +5). Edwin poured out his sleeping draught; Thomas watched.
Claims: n4_thomas_keeps (misleading): Simon does keep things, which is so; Thomas sent him out himself and says it to point at an innocent man. Pressing is the right read.

lines.text: (Fog presses at the infirmary window. Thomas is at his mortar, humming, as if it weren't there.)
Alric. Come in, and shut the door on that. It gets into the chest.
You're whole. I wasn't sure you would be, the way you came through that door last night.
If anyone asks, you were here with me, for your head. All night. It's true enough.
(He looks past you at the door, and lowers his voice.)
Brother. I've seen Brother Simon out at night. Long after Compline, when he should be abed.
I don't say what it means. Only, keep an eye on him.
You've thought on what I told you? About Simon?
(Thomas looks up from the mortar. His fingers are stained green to the knuckle.)
Back again? There's no supper to be late for tonight.

answers.text: What was Brother Simon doing out there?
I saw a bound man killed at the altar in the crypt.
How is Edwin?

lines.text: On his knees on the flags by the chapter house, his lantern hooded. At an hour nobody prays.
He's a quiet one, Simon. Quiet men keep things.

answers.text: I'll keep an eye on him, brother.
Simon? He sings, and keeps his head down. What would he keep?

lines.text: Watch him, Alric. Don't go to him. Watch.
That's for you to find, not me. I only tell you what I see.
Watch him, Alric. Don't go to him. Watch.
(He sets the pestle down very carefully, and hears you out.)
A man bound, at the saint's own altar. God have mercy on him.
Have you told the prior? Don't. Hugh would hang the porter for it and call it justice.
Leave it with me. You did right to bring it here.
He came to me this morning for something to help him sleep, and poured it out of the window. I watched him do it.
He listens to you. Tell him to come to me after Matins, if he can't sleep.
Keep it between us, Alric. About Simon.

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/anselm.tal.name: Brother Anselm
notes: Anselm at dusk, in his chair in the infirmary (night 5, clear and cold). Frightened. He has something to tell the porter,
and won't say it here: he can't see who's in the room. At Matins, where the singing covers a voice.
(At Matins he tells him the key to the crypt passage is in the granary. Nothing here says so.)

lines.text: (Anselm has turned toward the door before you reach it. His hand comes out and finds your sleeve.)
Porter. Closer.
There's a thing I should have told you the night you came. Not here. I can't see who's in the room.
(His hand finds your sleeve again, and holds it.)
Not here, I said. Not here.

answers.text: What do you have to tell me, brother?
What did you hear from the chapter house?
Did you know Edwin well, brother?

lines.text: At Matins. In the church, where the singing covers a man's voice. I'll find you.
(His grip tightens.)
Don't come asking again before then. Don't look at me in the choir.
A cry. Then feet, after. Not running, boy. Walking.
Men who know where they're going walk.
He read to me on Sundays. Psalms, and badly, and he laughed at his own mistakes.
They carried him past this door at Lauds. I knew who it was. Nobody else in this house would have been so light.
Matins, porter. Not before.

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/choirb.tal.name: Brother Aldo
notes: Brother Aldo in the nave at dusk (night 5, clear and cold), setting out the psalters. More stalls empty than full.
Wulfric, killed in the fog (died_fog_brother): Aldo came in a beat behind him at Matins. Simon slept in the next bed:
dead on the chapter house floor (died_simon), or alive and hiding at the back of the church.

lines.text: (Brother Aldo in the nave, setting out the psalters. There are more empty stalls than full ones now.)
Porter. I keep setting out too many. I count them, and then I count them again.
Still here? Help me count, then.

answers.text: I'm sorry about Brother Wulfric.
What of Brother Simon?

lines.text: Six years I came in a beat behind him at Matins. Last night there was nothing to come in behind.
I sang it alone, and flat. He'd have hated it.
His bed was next to mine. I've put his blanket over it, so I don't have to see it empty.
He's at the back of the church with his knees drawn up, like a child. He won't come into the choir, or say why.
Count us tonight, porter. Count carefully.

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/choirc.tal.name: Brother Piers
notes: Brother Piers on the east walk at dusk (night 5, clear and cold), looking at the chapter house door. Background; dry.
What the brothers say now (and what some say quietly), and whether he'll leave: he has nowhere to go.

lines.text: (Brother Piers on the east walk, his breath smoking in the cold. He's looking at the chapter house door.)
Clear tonight. You can see every star. I'd sooner have the fog back.
Still cold.

answers.text: What are the brothers saying?
Will you leave the abbey, brother?

lines.text: That it took the boy first because he was the youngest. That it walks in the fog. That it's no demon at all.
(He looks at you.)
Nobody says that last one loudly.
And go where? I've been in this house since I was nine. Outside that gate I'm a shaved head and no trade.
I'll stay. I'll keep a candle lit.
Keep warm, porter.

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/cole.talk.name: Cole
notes: Cole at dusk, keeping the gate (night 5, clear and cold). Lay brothers don't talk (Look and Feel, "Characters").

lines.text: (Cole in the open gateway, arms folded. The lane is clear and cold behind him, every lantern sharp. He says nothing.)

answers.text: Did you hear the cry from the chapter house?
I'll take the gate after supper.
Good evening, Brother Cole.

lines.text: (Cole looks at you, then back at the lane. He says nothing.)
(He says nothing. His hands, folded on his arms, are scrubbed red to the wrist.)

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/dunstan.ta.name: Dunstan
notes: Dunstan at dusk, by the woodpile (night 5, clear and cold). Lay brothers don't talk (Look and Feel, "Characters").

lines.text: (Dunstan is at the woodpile. The axe comes down, and down. He doesn't stop for you, and he says nothing.)

answers.text: Did you hear the cry from the chapter house?
Have you seen anyone about, brother?
Good night, Brother Dunstan.

lines.text: (Dunstan looks up from the block. He says nothing.)
(He says nothing. He sets a log on the block, and the axe comes down.)

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/godric.tal.name: Abbot Godric
notes: Abbot Godric at dusk, on his knees in the chapter house where it happened (night 5, clear and cold). Frail, sick from
the incense, praying. He names the dead: Edwin, Wulfric, and Simon if he died. He won't burn less incense, and won't
send for the bishop. (He collapses from the smoke at Matins tonight. Nothing here says so.)

lines.text: (The abbot kneels by the dark stain on the chapter house floor, lips moving. He coughs till he has to hold the bench.)
My son. No, leave me. I'll pray here, where it happened.
(The abbot hasn't moved. His breath rattles.)
Still here, child? Pray with me, then, or let me pray.

answers.text: Who are you praying for, Father Abbot?
Could you burn less incense, Father Abbot? It's making you ill.
Will you send for the bishop, Father Abbot?

lines.text: I've said their names at every office today. Edwin, who read so badly at table. Wulfric, here before me.
And Simon, here. On these stones. In my own chapter house.
Less? It's all that stands between this house and it.
(He coughs into his sleeve, and looks at what he's coughed.)
Ranulf says more. I'll give it more.
And tell him a demon walks in my house? He'd shut our doors and send our saint to Canterbury.
No. We'll bear it ourselves, as Our Lord bore it. God hasn't forgotten us.
Count us at Matins, my son. All that are left.

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/hugh.talk.name: Prior Hugh
notes: Prior Hugh at dusk, on the north walk (night 5, clear and cold). Grim; he means to see it ended tonight.
(He arrests the porter at dawn. Nothing here says so.) He knows what happened in the chapter house. The blood on his
sleeve (prior_sleeve): Wulfric's, and the porter was there first. Telling him what you've seen: Suspicion +10 (Ranulf overhears).
Claims: n5_hugh_porter (mistaken): whatever is killing his brothers came in with the porter.

lines.text: (The prior is on the north walk, his tablet shut in his hand for once. He looks as if he hasn't slept.)
Porter.
A brother's throat cut on the chapter house floor, and the porter in the door. Thomas says you saved his life.
Thomas is generous.
Brother Simon says you pulled the man off him. He'll say nothing else. He shakes when I ask him.
Five nights since you came to that gate, and I've buried more brothers than in five years.
It ends tonight. One way or another, I'll have a name by Lauds.
(He's writing on his tablet again, and doesn't look up.)
Go to your supper, porter.

answers.text: Whose blood is that on your sleeve, Father Prior?
I'll tell you what I've seen, Father Prior.
What do you mean to do, Father Prior?

lines.text: (He looks down at the sleeve. It's been scrubbed. The stain is still there.)
Wulfric's. I knelt by him in the fog. You saw me do it.
You were there before me, porter. You're always there before me.
(You tell him. He opens the tablet and writes until the wax is full.)
(Across the garth, someone moves out of the light and is gone.)
I've heard you. Whether I believe you is another matter. Go and keep your gate.
What a prior is for. Find who has been killing my brothers, and see him taken.
Keep to your gate tonight, porter. Keep to it, and I'll know where to find you.
Every death in this house since you came to that gate, and the porter there before me. Whatever is killing my brothers, it came in with you.

answers.text: God help me, Father Prior. Perhaps it did.
Then why am I not under lock, Father Prior?
The demon in the fog lost its mask, Father Prior. Under it was Brother Osric.

lines.text: Then pray on it, porter. You've until Lauds.
(He's quiet a moment.) You'd be under lock, if I were sure of it. I'm not.
One man didn't do all this, and I want every one of them. Go to your gate.
(He looks at you a long moment. Then he opens the tablet and writes one word. Across the garth, a door shuts softly.)
A face in the fog, from a porter who sees things in the smoke. It isn't enough.
But I'll look at Osric. Bring me something I can hold in my hand, porter, and I'll look at more.
Lauds, porter. I'll know by Lauds.

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/osric.talk.name: Brother Osric
notes: Osric at dusk, at the kitchen fire (night 5, clear and cold). The fast is over: bread tonight, and the heel kept back.
Smiling. If the porter saw his face under the mask last night (osric_mask), he knows this face; Osric acts as if nothing happened.
Where he was last night: the wrong question (Suspicion +5). Saying he saw his face: Suspicion +15, and Osric ends the talk.

lines.text: (Osric is at the kitchen fire, flour to the elbow, the smell of new bread all round him. He beams at you.)
The porter! The fast's done, God be thanked. Bread tonight, and I've kept the heel back for you.
(It's the face you saw in the fog last night, with the horns pushed back off it. It's smiling at you.)
Back again? You can smell it. Patience, porter. Not till the bell.

answers.text: Why was the fast lifted, brother?
Where were you last night, brother?
I saw your face in the fog last night, brother.

lines.text: Father Abbot lifted it after Prime. A night and a day of nothing, and half the house couldn't stand at Lauds.
Eat tonight, porter. All of it. You'll want your strength.
Abed, in the dormitory, listening to my belly. Like every Christian in the house. Where else would I be?
(He goes on kneading.)
Ask the brother in the next bed. He'll tell you how I snore.
(He laughs, a big warm laugh. The dough under his hands doesn't stop.)
My face? In the fog? Porter, you've been fasting. A hungry man sees faces in his porridge.
Eat your bread tonight. All of it. You'll see clearer for it.
The heel's yours, porter! Don't be late!

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/ranulf.tal.name: Brother Ranulf
notes: Ranulf at dusk, filling the censers in the choir (night 5, clear and cold). Smooth. (He wears the horned costume.)
The abbot sick from the smoke; where Ranulf was when Thomas was "attacked" (Suspicion +5); and, if the porter has
heard from Kit tonight that he bought no candles (lane_kit_5), the wrong question (Suspicion +10): we have all we need.

lines.text: (Ranulf is filling the censers from his leather bag. The church already smells of it, though Matins is hours off.)
Porter. Early again. You've made a habit of it.
(He hangs a censer on its hook and reaches for the next.)
Porter.

answers.text: The abbot can hardly breathe for the smoke.
Where were you when Brother Thomas was attacked?
Kit says you bought no candles today, brother.

lines.text: Then he should breathe deeper. It works on what's in the chest as well as what's in the house.
Father Abbot ordered it. I only burn it.
Here, at my candles, as I am every evening at that hour. I heard the cry, like everyone.
(He doesn't blink.)
And you, porter? Thomas says you were first through the door. You generally are.
(He stops with a censer in his hand.)
Kit should mind her tray.
We have all we need now, porter. That's all.
In the choir tonight, porter. Breathe deep.

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/simon.talk.name: Brother Simon
notes: Brother Simon at dusk, at the back of the nave (night 5, clear and cold). Only if the porter saved him (n5_saved=simon).
Shaking and grateful. He says little more than he told the porter in the chapter house: Thomas sent him to scrub the blood
(the thomas_sent_simon note). He asks the porter not to tell anyone. Where he scrubbed: a flag that rocked (the hidden body).
Claims: n5_simon_sent (true): Brother Thomas sent him to scrub the blood.

lines.text: (Brother Simon sits at the back of the nave, knees drawn up, a strip of linen at his neck where the knife touched him.)
(He flinches at your step, then sees who it is.)
Porter. Alric. I've not thanked you. I can't stop shaking long enough to thank you.
What I told you in the chapter house. Keep it. Please. Don't tell anyone I said it.
(Simon hasn't moved. He's watching the door.)
You came back. Nobody else has.

answers.text: Who sent you to scrub the blood, brother?
What were you really scrubbing, brother?
I'll keep it to myself, brother. I promise.

lines.text: I told you. Don't make me say it again.
(He looks past you at the door, and whispers it.)
Brother Thomas. He said it was for the good of the house. He said the abbot mustn't see it.

answers.text: I believe you, brother.
Brother Thomas? He's been nothing but kind to me.

lines.text: He was kind about it. He's always kind.
You believe me. I'd not have said it to another soul in this house.
He was kind about it. He's always kind.
You see? Nobody will believe it of him. Forget I said it.
Not wine. You knew it wasn't. It came up pink in the bucket, and then it wouldn't come up at all.
There was a flag that rocked when I knelt on it. I didn't lift it. I didn't want to know.
(He lets out a breath, and some of the shaking goes out with it.)
Thank you. I'll not go back to the dormitory. I'll sleep here, where the candles are.
Don't tell anyone. Please.

game/chapters/night5/dialogue/thomas.tal.name: Brother Thomas
notes: Thomas at dusk, on a bed in the infirmary, his head bandaged (night 5, clear and cold), after the dilemma.
Brave about his "wound". Saved (n5_saved=thomas), he thanks the porter; passed over for Simon (n5_saved=simon), he's hurt
and forgiving. His account of the attack points at the prior again. (The attack was staged. Nothing here says so.)
Osric's face (osric_mask): keep quiet and eat Osric's bread tonight (Suspicion +5). What Simon told him: a frightened man
names whoever you'll believe (Suspicion +10: the cult learns Simon talked). Simon scrubbing blood: he uses it.
Claims: n5_thomas_attack (lie): the man in the mask was as tall as the prior.

lines.text: (Thomas sits on the edge of a bed, his head bound in linen, a brown stain at the temple. He smiles when he sees you.)
Alric. I'd be dead on the chapter house floor but for you. I'll not forget it.
Poor Simon. I told you I'd seen him out at night. Whatever he'd got himself into, it came for him.
(Thomas sits on the edge of a bed, his head bound in linen, a brown stain at the temple. He looks at you, then smiles.)
You went to Simon. I saw you choose, from the floor.
No, don't. You reached for the nearer man. I'm alive, as you see. I've a thick skull.
(Thomas sits on the edge of a bed, his head bound in linen, a brown stain coming through at the temple.)
Don't look so, Alric. A cut to the scalp bleeds like a pig and means nothing.
(Thomas has lain back against the wall with his eyes shut. He opens them when you come in.)
Alric. Still here? Sit, if you like. I'm no use for anything else tonight.

answers.text: What happened in the chapter house, brother?
The hunter in the fog was Brother Osric. I saw his face.
What of Brother Simon?

lines.text: I heard Simon cry out and went in. A man in the mask was over him. Something struck me from behind. Then the floor.
The one I saw was tall, Alric. As tall as the prior. I'll say no more than that, God forgive me if I'm wrong.

answers.text: God keep you, brother. I'll watch the prior.
You were struck from behind, brother. How well did you see him?
The one in the fog last night wasn't the prior. It was Brother Osric. I saw his face.

lines.text: Watch him, then. But say nothing to him. I've no proof, and he's the prior.
Well enough. In the door, before I was struck. I know what I saw, Alric.
Let me rest now. My head.
(For a moment his face is nothing at all.)
The prior was in my head, Alric. A man sees what he fears, in the dark.
(He's very still.)
Osric. Who carried the merchant from the pond. Who bakes our bread.
Say nothing to him. Eat what he gives you tonight, and let him think you saw nothing.
I'll think what's to be done.
I keep seeing him on those flags. A gentle soul, whatever he'd got into. I wish to God I'd been wrong about him.
How is he? He won't look at me. He hasn't since the chapter house.

answers.text: Brother Simon says you sent him to scrub the blood.
I found Brother Simon scrubbing blood off the stones.
(Say nothing more about it.)

lines.text: (A long silence. He turns the bandage at his temple with one finger.)
That I sent him. I've seen men in a fever name their own mothers, Alric.
A frightened man says the name he thinks you'll believe, and he knows you trust me.
Ask him where he was every night this week.
(He shuts his eyes.)
Scrubbing blood. Then he was in it, whatever it is. God rest him anyway.
Scrubbing blood. Ask yourself why a man scrubs blood in the dark, and whose name he gives when he's caught.
Sit by me at supper, Alric. I want a look at your eyes.

game/chapters/night6/dialogue/godric.tal.name: Abbot Godric
notes: Abbot Godric at dusk, sick in his bed since he fell in the smoke at Matins (night 6, snow). Thomas brings him something
hot at every bell, and he sleeps and wakes and doesn't know what's happening: why there's no bell, whether it's morning.
He doesn't know Anselm is dead: Thomas told him Anselm sleeps sound at last. Telling him what his brothers are: he
thinks the porter is feverish, sends him to Thomas, and will tell Thomas he's coming (Suspicion +5).

lines.text: (The abbot lies in his bed under a heap of blankets, his beads in his fingers, his lips moving. His breath rattles.)
My son? Is it Matins? I didn't hear the bell.
Thomas says I'm not to trouble about Matins. He says the house can sing without me for one night.
(The abbot has slipped down in the bed. He opens his eyes, and takes a while to find you.)
Who is it? Oh. The porter. Is it morning?

answers.text: How are you, Father Abbot?
Have you heard about Brother Anselm, Father Abbot?
Father Abbot, your brothers are not what they seem.

lines.text: Thomas says it's the smoke, in my chest. He brings me something hot at every bell, and I sleep.
I sleep so much, child. I dream I'm awake, and then I wake, and it's the same room.
Anselm? Thomas sat with him through Vespers. He says Anselm sleeps sound at last, poor soul, like a child.
Thirty years at our gate, and never a whole night's sleep. Let him have it.
(He hears you out. Then he laughs, weakly, and it turns into coughing.)
My brothers? Child, you're feverish. Thomas said you might be.
Go to him. He'll give you something to help you sleep. I'll tell him you're coming.
Pray for the house, my son. I can't seem to keep hold of the words.

game/chapters/night6/dialogue/hugh.talk.name: Prior Hugh
notes: Prior Hugh at dusk, at the porter's cell door with a lantern (night 6, snow). Only if he believed the porter at dawn
(prior_believes): he stands with him tonight. Grim and practical: where the proof is (down the hidden stair with the
key from the rye; two kinds), the gate (Cole holds it and won't open), Roger (a bad bargain, maybe the only one).
With the thomas_sent_simon note he joins Anselm's death to Thomas. He warns that a lantern looking for the porter
may be his. (At Dose 75+ he is the demon who corners the porter with a light. Nothing here says so.)
Claims: n6_hugh_lantern (true): a lantern looking for the porter tonight may be his.

lines.text: (The prior is at your door with a lantern, snow on his hood. He looks as if he hasn't slept since he let you go.)
Up, porter. No bell tonight, no supper. The abbot is sick in his bed and doesn't know what day it is.
Anselm is dead. Henbane packed into his mouth like straw. Somebody heard him talk.
Henbane, in the infirmary, and only Thomas keeps that key. And Simon says Thomas sent him to scrub the blood.
I'm not blind, porter. Only slow.
(The prior is trimming his lantern's wick with a thumbnail. He doesn't look up.)
Well? We haven't the night to stand here.

answers.text: Where do I look for proof, Father Prior?
Who has the gate tonight, Father Prior?
Will Roger help us, Father Prior?

lines.text: That key you pulled out of the rye opens the closet in the granary. The stair behind it goes down under the nave.
Whatever they keep, they keep down there. Bring up two kinds of thing, not two of a kind. One proves nothing.
Cole has the gate, and Cole won't open it. Not for you, not for me. Not for the abbot, if he could stand.
I'll be about the court with a light. If a lantern comes looking for you tonight, it may be mine. Look before you run.

answers.text: I'll look, Father Prior.
And how would I know it's yours, in the dark?

lines.text: Good. Then we may both see Lauds.
By looking. I've said it once, porter.
Roger's men have been in the Keys since noon. He's wanted this ground since before I was prior.
Give him proof and he'll hang them, and take the house for his trouble. A bad bargain. It may be the only one left.
Keep off the open garth, porter. In this snow they'll follow your feet.

game/chapters/night6/dialogue/simon.talk.name: Brother Simon
notes: Brother Simon at dusk, hiding at the back of the nave where he slept last night (night 6, snow). Only if the porter
saved him on night 5 (n5_saved=simon). Frightened; he knows they'll come for him again, and he'd sooner help than wait.
He knows the crypt passage: Thomas sent him down with candles for the ring (the crypt_candles note), and said, the
last time, only one more. He can follow the porter or wait for him ([follow], [wait]; n6_simon_with).
(He is the rite's last soul at Matins if the cult takes him. Nothing here says so.)

lines.text: (Brother Simon is crouched in the dark at the back of the nave, his hood up. He's on his feet before you can speak.)
Porter. They're all out. I watched them go past the door in their horns, and not one of them was hurrying.
They'll come for me again tonight. I know it. Let me help you. I can't sit here and wait for it.
(Simon is back in the dark, hugging himself, watching the door.)
Something went by while you were gone. I didn't look.

answers.text: What do you know of the crypt passage, brother?
Come with me, Brother Simon.
Wait for me here, Brother Simon.

lines.text: Thomas sent me down there with candles, twice since Michaelmas. A door in the granary closet that looks like the planks.
Then a stair, and a long passage under the nave. Pegs on the wall with things hung on them, and a chest. I didn't look.
I set the candles in the ring by the altar, as I was told. More of them were lit each time.
The last time, he said only one more now. I didn't ask him one more what.
(He swallows, and pushes back his hood.)
I'll come. I know that stair in the dark. Only don't leave me anywhere alone.
(He tries to smile, and can't.)
Here, then. I'll keep to the dark. Come back for me, porter.
Porter? Don't be long. Please.

game/chapters/common/lane/agnes.talk.name: Agnes
notes: Agnes at the door of the Cross Keys at dusk, nights 1 to 6, while the abbey gate stands open.
She carries the lane's talk of the turned away (before the bell they sleep at the Keys; after it the Keys is shut) and of the locked guesthouse.
The Keys is open: an ale every night, and it ends the talk.
Her own flags: lane_agnes_<night> (talked to her tonight), lane_agnes_n<night>_<topic> (asked).

lines.text: There's my lodger. They're feeding you over there, I hope?
(A woman in the inn's doorway, shaking out a cloth.)
You'll be the new porter. I'm Agnes. Hob's wife, God help me.
Brother.
Back again? You'll wear out my step.
(She fetches a cup from inside and puts it into your hands.)
The Keys is open, brother. Drink it slow.
Your room's still there if they turn you out. I've not let it.
And if you've a soul to send away, send them across before the bell. After it, the door's barred to God himself.

answers.text: They've given me a cell by the gate.
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: By the gate. You'll see who comes, then. Mind you see who goes, too.
The merchant you turned away slept upstairs here. Grumbled all night. Better grumbling than in that place.
Send them to us before the bell, brother, and there's always a bed.
Your merchant came hammering on our door after the bell. Hob wouldn't unbar it. Rules are rules.
He sat in our doorway till the light, cursing us. Lucky, Gib says. Send them before nine, brother.
That poor man in your pond. He had good fur on his cloak at your gate, Mab says. Did they bury him in it?
A quiet night, for once. Hob says that's when to worry.

answers.text: Where does Jankin sleep at night?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: Jankin? Hob puts him out at the bell, every night God sends. He's soft about everything but his rules.
If you want Jankin kept in, ask Hob, not me. He might, for you.
Turned away after the bell, poor soul, and the Keys was shut. They found him in the gutter.
Send them to us before nine, brother. Before nine, and we'll take them in.
Hob hasn't said a word since they carried Jankin off. Not one.
(She looks back into the dark of the inn.)
Jankin's still asleep under my table. Hob kept him in, for you. Don't tell him I said it was kind.
The rain's stopped, at least. Small mercies.

answers.text: Are you afraid?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: Of course I'm afraid. I've a lane full of fools to feed. Being afraid doesn't bake the bread.
That pilgrim who lodged with us and went in at your gate. His bed's still made. I can't bring myself to strip it.
There's fog coming up off the river tonight. Keep your guests close, brother.

answers.text: Do you lock your doors at night?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: Lock them? I bar them, from the inside, every night. Hob has keys, and so did his father, and God knows who else.
A key's only as good as the hands it's been in. A bar is mine.
They say the guesthouse door was locked, and it made no difference. Whoever goes in there has keys.
If a guest of yours must stay, tell him to bar it from inside.
Your guest last night barred his own door, he says, and sat up with a knife till dawn.
He's gone home to Kent, and he won't be back.
And a boy. They say a boy of yours was laid out in the bone house.
(She crosses herself.)
God rest him. He was somebody's son.
You look worse every dusk, brother. Are you sleeping at all?

answers.text: Pray for our dead.
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: I've prayed for your dead every night since Martinmas, brother. I'm running out of names.
Snow.
(She pulls her shawl tight and looks at the abbey wall.)
Whatever it is you've got in there, brother, keep your gate shut on it.

answers.text: What do you think it is?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: I don't think. I bake, and I bar the door, and I don't look out of that top window.
You looked out of it, your first night. I saw your face in the morning.
Before nine, mind!

game/chapters/common/lane/carter.talk.name: the carter
notes: The carter passing through the lane with his wagon at dusk, nights 1 to 6: a line a night.
His own flags: lane_carter_<night> (talked to him tonight).

lines.text: (The carter, walking at his horse's head, his wagon empty.)
Porter. They kept you, then.
(A carter walking at his horse's head, his wagon empty.)
(The carter, walking at his horse's head.)
I've said my piece, porter.
You've the look of it already. Pale. They'll have you white as a tallow candle by Advent.

answers.text: Where are you bound?

lines.text: Out through Aldgate before they shut it. I don't sleep inside these walls. Not any more.
That merchant of yours. I passed him on the road yesterday, singing. A voice like a bull.
Roads are soup from here to Mile End.

answers.text: Go carefully.

lines.text: Always do. That's why I'm still carting.
Jankin. I carted his barrels, once, when he made barrels. Before his wife went.
No pilgrims on the road today. Not one. Word's getting about.

answers.text: Word of what?

lines.text: Of your abbey, porter. What else is there?
Fog on the road, thick as fleece. I near put the wagon in the ditch by the white chapel.
(He crosses himself.)
There's been enough in that ditch.

answers.text: God keep you on the road.

lines.text: Keep your blessings for them inside, porter. They need them more.
I'm not stopping tonight. Last load, then I'm out of the gate, and I'll not be back till it's over.

answers.text: Till what's over?

lines.text: Whatever this is.
Snow. I'll be lucky to get the wagon through Aldgate in this.
(He looks at your face a long moment.)
There's room on the back, porter. Same as there was coming in.

answers.text: I can't.
(Shake your head.)

lines.text: No. I didn't think so.
Mind yourself, porter.

game/chapters/common/lane/gib.talk.name: Gib the watchman
notes: Gib the watchman lighting the lanterns along the lane at dusk, nights 1 to 6.
After a lane death he's the one who found the body or heard the cry. He always reminds the porter of the bell.
His own flags: lane_gib_<night> (talked to him tonight), lane_gib_n<night>_<topic> (asked).

lines.text: Brother. Still in one piece. Good.
(An old man on a short ladder, coaxing a lantern alight.)
Gib, the watch. Mind my ladder, brother.
Brother.
Still here? I've lanterns to light.
Quiet night, last night. Quiet as I like it. Bar a fox crying over your wall, round midnight.

answers.text: A fox?
When do you start calling?

lines.text: Must have been. What else cries like that, at that hour?
(He goes up his ladder and doesn't look down.)
At the bell. Nine, and then every hour till the light.
You'll hear me from your gate. Listen for me, brother.
Rain again. Keeps the lanterns spitting.
After the bell there's nobody in this lane but me. Nobody should be.

answers.text: What if someone's out after the bell?

lines.text: Then I tell him to get indoors, and I walk on. I'm one old man with a lantern, brother.
Send them to the Keys while the Keys is open.
It was me found Jankin. Two o'clock, in the gutter by the chandler's.
I called the hour and he didn't answer. He always answered. Is it, Gib, he'd say. Is it all well?
(The taper shakes in his hand, and he has to light it again.)
It was me found him. The poor soul who was turned off at your gate after the bell.
In the gutter, under my own lantern. I heard him cry out, and I was three houses off. Three houses.
It was me found him, in the gutter under my own lantern. I heard him cry out. I was three houses off.
Something went past me last night, at three. Close as you are now.
I never saw it. I smelled it. Like a church.
Bell's at nine. Be behind your gate when it goes, and keep it barred.

answers.text: Will you still walk the lane tonight?

lines.text: Mayor pays me to. Every hour, till the light.
You listen for me, brother. If I stop calling, I've stopped.
Fog's coming up off the river. I'll not see one lantern from the next tonight.
And I heard running over your wall last night. Running, in an abbey, at two in the morning.

answers.text: It was me.
You must have dreamed it.

lines.text: Then God help you, brother, whatever it was behind you.
I don't sleep on the watch, brother. That's the whole of the job.
Heard a cry over your wall last night, in the fog. Then nothing.
I called the hour twice over, to be sure I was still there.
And Mab's place by your gate was empty at midnight. First time in all my years on this lane.
Bell at nine, brother. Same as ever.

answers.text: Keep an eye on my gate tonight.

lines.text: I always do. From the far side of the lane, mind.
It was me found the bailiff's man. His lantern out, and him by your gate, where he'd stood all night.
He'd been calling at your grille. I heard him from the corner. Then he stopped.
The bailiff's man sat inside your gate all night, they say. Good. That's one I didn't find.
Snow. You'll see every footprint in the lane tonight. Mine, and whatever else walks it.
Be behind your gate at the bell, brother. Tonight of all nights.

answers.text: Call the hour for me tonight.

lines.text: Every hour, till the light. Listen for me.
Behind your gate at the bell, brother!

game/chapters/common/lane/hob.talk.name: Hob
notes: Hob at the door of the Cross Keys at dusk, nights 1 to 6, while the abbey gate stands open.
Each night he passes on what the lane says about the night before, then the night's questions.
The Keys is open: an ale every night, and it ends the talk. Night 2: he can be asked to keep Jankin in (n2_jankin_kept_in).
His own flags: lane_hob_<night> (talked to him tonight), lane_hob_n<night>_<topic> (asked).
Claims: n4_hob_walter (hiding: what Walter said over his ale on night 3).

lines.text: Brother porter. So they kept you.
(A big man fills the inn's doorway, a cloth over his shoulder.)
You'll be the new porter. I'm Hob. The Keys is mine.
Brother.
Still here? The bell won't wait for you.
(He reaches inside the door for a cup and fills it on the step.)
The Keys is open, brother. Drink it before the bell.
You've the look of a man who slept in his clothes. How do you find it over there?

answers.text: They've been kind to me.
If I turn someone away, where do they go?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: Kind. Aye, they're kind at the gate, that lot. It's past the gate I'd wonder about.
Here, if they've sense. Send them across before the bell and Agnes will find them a bed.
After the bell I bar the door, and it stays barred. I'd not open it for the mayor.
That merchant who went in at your gate. They pulled him out of your fishpond this morning, they say.
The old porter used to lock his guests in at night, you know. Nobody does now.
The bailiff was in at noon, asking after him. He'll be at your gate tonight.
Your merchant came by at first light, hale, cursing your porter for locking him in like a sheep.
Paid for his ale, at least, and went off grumbling to Cheapside.
(Through the door behind him, Jankin is already singing.)
Hark at him. I'll put him out at closing, same as every night. Rain or no.

answers.text: Will you keep Jankin in tonight?
Why do you put Jankin out?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: Keep him in? The Keys shuts at the bell, brother. Everybody out but them that pay.
(He looks past you at the abbey wall, and his jaw works.)
Fine. One night. He can snore on the bench. But you'll say a prayer for my rushes.
Because the Keys shuts at the bell, and a man who doesn't pay doesn't sleep in it.
He beds down on the chandler's step. Twenty years, and he's come to no harm.
I put Jankin out at closing, same as every night. Gib found him in the gutter by the chandler's.
(He wipes his hands on the cloth, though they're dry.)
I should have kept him in.
Kept Jankin in, like you asked. Snored on my bench till dawn.
Something walked the lane last night. I heard it go past the shutters. I didn't look.
And a brother of yours hanged in your own bell tower, they say. Your abbot's telling the lane it's the devil.
Is it, brother? You'd know. You're the one who rings that bell.
Quiet in the Keys last night. Nobody wants to drink across from your wall any more.

answers.text: Do you believe it's the devil?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: I believe in what I pour and what I'm paid.
(His eyes go to the abbey wall.)
And I bar my shutters.
Walter was in last night before he went over to you. Paid for his ale in silver.
Silver, from a pardoner. I bit it. It was good.

answers.text: What else is the lane saying?
What did Walter say over his ale?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: Walter? What he always says. Relics, and the price of them.

answers.text: You hear everything said over that counter, Hob. What else?
Then it's nothing.

lines.text: (He looks up and down the lane before he answers.)
He said your abbey's his best custom. Better than every shrine in Kent.
I asked him what for. He laughed, and paid, and went over to you.
Nothing. Like I said.
That your abbot has the house fasting against the devil. Kit had it from your kitchen door.
And that another pilgrim went in at your gate and hasn't come out. But they always say that.
They're saying a young one of yours was found in the bone house. Laid out among the bones.
And another in your cloister, in the fog. I've stopped counting, brother. Has your abbot?
The fog's lifted. The lane's waiting to hear what it left behind.

answers.text: What would you do, in my place?
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: In your place? I'd walk out of that gate and keep walking till I smelled the sea.
(He looks at you a while.)
But you won't. Your sort never do.
The bailiff's man who stood at your gate all night. They found his lantern out and him in the lane.
He was calling to you, brother. I heard him from my bed. Why didn't you let him in?
Roger's man was in at first light, white as milk. Says you let him sit inside your gate all night.
Says something walked the lane past your grille, and he didn't breathe till it had gone.
Snow tonight. I'm barring the Keys early, bell or no bell.

answers.text: Pray for us tonight.
An ale, if you would.

lines.text: I gave up praying, brother. It never paid.
But Agnes hasn't. I'll tell her to say your name.
Bell's at nine, brother.

game/chapters/common/lane/kit.talk.name: Kit
notes: Kit selling candles at the abbey gate at dusk, nights 1 to 6. She notices the sacrist buying more and more (the crypt's candles; nothing here says so).
Her own flags: lane_kit_<night> (talked to her tonight), lane_kit_n<night>_<topic> (asked); lane_kit_n4_look if he promises to look for the candles.
Claims: n5_kit_candles (hiding: what her father did when Ranulf stopped buying).

lines.text: Porter! You're still here. I bet Gib a farthing you'd run.
(A girl with a tray of candles on a strap round her neck.)
Candles, porter? I'm Kit. Ralph the chandler's girl. I'm at your gate most dusks.
Porter!
You again! You can't buy anything, can you. You're a monk.
Well? What's it like in there? Did you see the finger? Is it real?

answers.text: Not yet.
Who buys your candles?

lines.text: Not yet! You live there. I'd have seen it the first morning. I'd have touched it.
Brother Ranulf, mostly. He takes the whole tray most dusks now.
Father says they used to make one candle last a week over there.
Brother Ranulf took the whole tray again at noon. I had to go back for more, just to have something to stand here with.
Is it true about the man in your fishpond? Margery says he was in there all night with his eyes open.

answers.text: What does he want with so many?

lines.text: I asked him. He said, for the saint.
The saint must be awful dark down there, to want all that.
He wants them by the dozen now, Father says. Not by the pound. By the dozen, like eggs.
Did you really find him? The brother in the tower? Father says I'm not to ask you.

answers.text: I did.
Your father's right.
What does your father make of it?

lines.text: (For once, she says nothing at all.)
Was he heavy? Sorry. I don't know why I asked that.
He always is. It's very tiresome.
He says it's good for trade and he doesn't like it. Both at once. That's Father.
Eleven extra this week, Father says. On top of the usual. He writes it all down, he can't help it.
Where do they put them all? You'd know. You walk round in the night.

answers.text: I don't know.
I'll look.

lines.text: A porter who doesn't know where the candles go. Father would laugh.
You'll tell me? Promise. Not Father. Just me.
Brother Ranulf didn't come for any candles today. First day since Michaelmas.
Father says they must have all they need, now. He said it funny.
And Father says another brother's dead. He won't tell me which.

answers.text: It was Edwin.
Go home before dark, Kit.
All they need for what?

lines.text: For the saint, I suppose. That's all Father said.

answers.text: That isn't all, Kit. What did he do?
Then that's all it is.

lines.text: (She looks back up the lane toward the chandler's.)
He got his book out and counted back to Michaelmas, every candle. Then he shut it and crossed himself.
Father never crosses himself. Not even in church.
That's all. Buy a candle, or let me go home.
Edwin. I didn't know his name.
(She looks down at the tray.)
I should have asked him his name.
I always go home before dark. You sound like Father.
Father's shut the shop and he's on his knees. He never prays. Not even at Easter.
You'll be all right, won't you? Porter?

answers.text: Go home, Kit.
I'll be all right.

lines.text: I'm going.
(She doesn't move.)
I'm going.
You're a terrible liar, porter. For a monk.
See you tomorrow, porter!

game/chapters/common/lane/mab.talk.name: Mab
notes: Mab by the abbey gate at dusk, nights 1 to 6. She sees who comes and goes, nobody asks her, and she never eats the abbey's bread: the porter's reality check.
Alms once a night (mab_alms_<night>): a heel of Fenchurch Street bread for him, and a little trust. Greets him warmly at trust 30, coldly below 0.
Her own flags: lane_mab_<night> (talked to her tonight), lane_mab_bread, lane_mab_n<night>_<topic> (asked).

lines.text: Brother porter. So they let you in after all.
(A woman sits against the wall by the gate, a clapper in her lap, her face wrapped to the eyes.)
Alms, porter? Stand off a little. I'm Mab. I'm always here.
Porter.
(She lifts the clapper and knocks it once, softly, like a greeting.)
There's my porter.
(She doesn't look up when you come.)
Porter.
Still here? I'm not going anywhere, porter.
(You drop a coin in the bowl at her feet.)
God keep you, porter. Here. Fenchurch Street bread, not theirs.
(She sets a heel of bread on the step between you, wrapped in a cloth, and draws back.)
Their bread? Never. Not a crumb, and I've been hungry enough to eat straw.
They hand it out at the gate on feast days. I give mine to the rooks.
Then the rooks sit on your wall and scream at nothing.
Your first night at the gate. I'll be on this side of it, if you want me.
If you must turn a soul away, do it before the bell. The Keys takes them in till nine.
After that, it's the lane.

answers.text: (Give her alms.)
What do you watch for?

lines.text: Faces. Who goes in, who comes out. Who goes in and doesn't.
You'd be surprised what nobody notices, porter.
No one came to your gate last night. No one.
I heard the knock, same as you. I was looking right at the gate, porter. There was nobody there.

answers.text: I believe you.
You must have dozed.

lines.text: (She's quiet a long while behind the cloth.)
Nobody's said that to me in eleven years.
I don't doze, porter. Not out here. Not at your gate.
I saw your merchant go in. I never saw him come out. Then this morning they said the pond.
Your first night done, and you're still standing. That's more than some.

answers.text: (Give her alms.)
Do you eat the abbey's bread?

lines.text: I saw it, last night. Under Gib's lantern, by the chandler's.
Tall. Taller than any man. It came from the corner of your wall, and it went back the same way.
Nobody's asked me. Gib's told it three times over, and Gib never saw a thing.
Nobody died in the lane last night. Something walked it, though. I kept very still.
The rooks came off your tower before Matins, all at once, screaming. Before your bell, porter. Not after.

answers.text: (Give her alms.)
Do you eat the abbey's bread?

lines.text: You came to the grille last night and looked down at your feet, at nothing.
There was nothing there, porter. No child. No dog. I was watching.
Walter came by with his bag. It smelled of your Matins before ever he reached your gate.
And a pilgrim went in by day, yesterday. A man with a staff and a limp. I've not seen him come out.

answers.text: (Give her alms.)
Do you eat the abbey's bread?
Are you frightened, Mab?

lines.text: (A dry little laugh behind the cloth.)
Frightened? I'm a leper, porter. What's left to take?
Ask me again tonight.
You let me in last night. Inside your walls.
(She looks at the bars of the gate, and doesn't touch them.)
I'll not go in again, porter. Not for bread, not for blessing.
Three of them, by the mill race. I saw what I saw.
You left me out in that fog. I sat against your gate all night with my clapper in my lap.
Three of them went by, out by the mill race. Three, porter. I didn't breathe.

answers.text: (Give her alms.)
Do you eat the abbey's bread?
Tell the prior what you saw.

lines.text: The prior? He'd have me whipped out of the lane for a liar. Nobody listens to a leper.
Only you. And you're nobody either, porter. No offence.
The bailiff's man stood right there all night, calling at your grille. I told him to keep his back to the wall.
Then his lantern went out. I didn't see what came. I heard it, and that was enough.
You let the bailiff's man in. Good. An hour after, something stood at your grille where he'd been, looking in.
It stood there a long while, porter. Then it went away up the lane.
Snow tonight. It'll show me everyone who comes and goes. It'll show them me, too.

answers.text: (Give her alms.)
Do you eat the abbey's bread?
Go somewhere warm tonight, Mab.

lines.text: (Something like a laugh, behind the cloth.)
Where would a leper go that's warm, porter? I'll be here. I'm always here.
God keep you, porter.

game/chapters/common/lane/margery.talk.name: Margery
notes: Margery hurrying home through the lane at dusk, nights 1 to 6: a line or two of gossip a night, and she's gone.
Her own flags: lane_margery_<night> (talked to her tonight).

lines.text: (Margery, her basket on her arm, walking fast.)
(A woman with a covered basket on her arm, walking fast.)
Margery, brother, from by Saint Andrew's. I can't stop.
(Margery, her basket on her arm, hurrying past.)
Brother, I've told you all I know, and more!
You're still with us, then, brother. The lane's been wondering.

answers.text: Wondering what?

lines.text: How long you'd last. Oh, don't look at me like that. I'm late.
A man in your fishpond! Drowned drunk, your infirmarian says.
Drunk! He went past my door as sober as a bishop.
Rain again. I'll be soaked through by the corner, and the long way round to go.

answers.text: Go carefully.

lines.text: Carefully, in these pattens, in this mud? Pray for me, brother.
Hanged in his own bell tower, a holy brother! Your abbot says the devil did it.
Devil or rope, he's dead all the same.
I'm not stopping, brother. Not this week.
And poor Jankin. He owed me tuppence. I'd forgive it twice over to have him back.

answers.text: Go safely.

lines.text: Safely! There's no safely, brother. There's quickly.
Your abbot has you all fasting, they say. Fasting against the devil.
My gran fasted every Friday of her life, and the devil took her husband anyway.

answers.text: Good night, Margery.

lines.text: Good night! I'll settle for a night, brother. Never mind good.
You let the leper in! Inside your walls! The whole lane's talking of it.
Well. I'd not leave a dog out in that fog either. Don't tell anyone I said so.
That poor young brother. They say he was laid among the bones as if somebody put him to bed.
And I'm not stopping. Not with the light going.

answers.text: Who says so?
Go home, Margery.

lines.text: Everybody. Nobody knows who said it first. That's how you know it's true.
I'm going! What do you think I'm doing?
Snow! Every step I take, written down for anyone to follow.
(She looks back over her shoulder at her own footprints.)
God keep you tonight, brother. I mean it.

answers.text: And you, Margery.

lines.text: Me? I'll be under three blankets with the door barred. You're the one who'll be out in it.
God keep you!

clues.window_killing: From my window at the Cross Keys I saw a man killed by the well in the abbey's court. A figure in a black habit, its back to me, dragged him toward the cellar.
clues.window_killing_drunk: From my window at the Cross Keys I saw a man killed by the well in the abbey's court, I think. I'd drunk too much to be sure what I saw.
clues.sand_by_the_well: Sand on the court by the well this morning, where I saw the man killed. Thomas says a beast was slaughtered there.
clues.bread_warning: A brother of the choir told me at supper not to eat the bread. Something is wrong with it.
clues.knock_no_one: A knock at the gate after midnight. No one there. Mab saw no one come.
clues.merchant_rope: Rope marks on the merchant's wrists. A man who falls in a pond drunk doesn't tie his own hands.
clues.merchant_purse: The merchant's purse is gone. He had it at the gate.
clues.merchant_moved: I went for help and the merchant's body was gone from the pond when I came back.
clues.sailor_knot: The brother in the bell tower hangs from a sailor's knot. The only sailor this week came to my gate.
clues.ledger_torn: A page is gone from my ledger. The guesthouse has one more empty bed than I wrote.
clues.oven_badge: A pilgrim's badge, melted in the oven ash. The name on it was torn from my ledger.
clues.crypt_book: A page from a book, by the crypt altar: ten candles drawn in a ring, and a soul for each.
clues.crypt_candles: Candles burning in the crypt, in a ring. More of them each night.
clues.keys_moved: My keys were moved in the night. There's wax in the teeth: someone took a mould of them.
clues.incense_bag: Walter's bag smells of the incense they burn at Matins.
clues.anselm_henbane: Anselm dead in his bed, his mouth stuffed with henbane leaves. Only Thomas keeps the infirmary.
clues.edwin_comb: Edwin's wounds are in rows, too even for claws. Like a wool-carding comb.
clues.edwin_moved: I went for help and Edwin was gone from the charnel house when I came back.
clues.guest_moved: The guest's body was gone from the guesthouse when I came back with help.
clues.osric_mask: The demon's mask came off in the fog. It was Brother Osric.
clues.two_demons: I saw it in two places at once. There is more than one of them.
clues.prior_sleeve: Blood on the prior's sleeve. He was kneeling by the body when I came.
clues.simon_blood: Brother Simon on his knees on the cloister flags, scrubbing blood. He hid the rag.
clues.thomas_sent_simon: Simon says Thomas sent him to scrub the blood.
clues.hoof_print: A hoof print in the mud. Carved wood, with the marks of the straps that tie it to a boot.
clues.ergot_rye: The rye in the granary is black-spurred. That is what is in our bread.
clues.well_badge: A body down the well, with a pilgrim's badge. The name on it was torn from my ledger.
clues.race_badge: A body in the mill race culvert, with a pilgrim's badge. The name was torn from my ledger.
clues.garden_badge: A body under the kitchen beds, freshly dug, with a pilgrim's badge. Another torn name.
clues.loft_badge: A body in the bell tower loft, with a pilgrim's badge. Another torn name.
clues.chapter_badge: A body under the chapter house flags, where Simon was scrubbing. Another torn name.
